instructions:
## The project being researched

An XGBoost "virtual sensor" for Iowa stream nitrate: predict at locations with NO physical sensor, using only weather + land-use data. Two targets:
- REGRESSION: daily-max nitrate concentration (mg/L)
- CLASSIFICATION (the primary one): binary `violation` = daily max >= 10 mg/L, base rate 0.263

~85 sensor sites, 160,074 site-days, 2008-2026. Each site has a delineated upstream drainage basin. Features are aggregated over basin cells in distance buckets from the outlet.

## THE DEPLOYMENT TARGET - judge every recommendation against this
The shipped product takes an ARBITRARY MAP PIN anywhere in Iowa, delineates its upstream basin on the fly via USGS NLDI, builds features from weather and land use alone, and predicts daily violation probability. There is NO nitrate history at the target location, NO discharge gauge there, and NO guarantee of a monitored neighbor upstream. Any method that requires the target site's own observations, or requires a gauged upstream site, DOES NOT WORK for this product - it may still be useful for other purposes, but that limitation must be stated explicitly and prominently.

## Current honest performance (leave-one-basin-family-out, LOFO)
- CLF: AUC 0.820, PR-AUC 0.634 (2.41x lift over base rate), recall 0.524 at 10% false-alarm rate, MCC 0.466, Brier 0.137
- REG: R2 0.328, RMSE 4.36 mg/L
- Deployed at beta=2: recall 0.864, but 59% of alarms are false

## THE CENTRAL PROBLEM: the model cannot rank sites
- within_r2 0.42 vs between_r2 0.21
- macro_auc 0.90 vs between_rate_r2 0.24
The project's own summary: "a good timer, a mediocre site-ranker." It captures WHEN nitrate rises at a given site, but fails at the ABSOLUTE LEVEL of an unseen basin. Essentially all remaining headroom is in the between-site term.

## CRITICAL SAMPLE-SIZE CONSTRAINT
The ~85 sites collapse to only 19 INDEPENDENT BASIN FAMILIES under the leak-safe CV (sites whose basins nest and whose records overlap in time are grouped). So learning a site's absolute level is a regression with roughly 19 effective independent units, NOT 160k rows. Any method whose published gains come from hundreds of catchments (e.g. CAMELS with 531-671 basins) must be explicitly flagged as possibly infeasible here.

## Current features (68 for CLF)
9 weather variables x 3 distance buckets (SAME-DAY SCALARS ONLY), 8 CDL crop classes x 3 buckets, 2 nitrogen-surplus x 3 buckets, doy_sin/doy_cos, 4 cross-site nitrate lags (rest_of_state_nitrate_lag1/2/3/5), 5 static (lat, lon, log_basin_area, mean_dist_to_sensor, max_dist_to_sensor).
Top features by permutation importance: rest_of_state_nitrate_lag1, lon, lat, doy_sin, fuel_moisture_1000h. BOTTOM: all daily weather; precip_in_1d is dead last (perm ~0.000).

## KNOWN NEGATIVE RESULTS - do not naively re-propose these
- Lagged weather copies: HURT badly (loso_r2 0.116 -> 0.019)
- Rolling precip / water balance as implemented: worse (lofo_r2 0.013 vs 0.003)
- Broadcasting 2017 N-surplus forward in time: much worse (-0.166)
- Rolling (3D/7D) smoothed targets: worse
- Spike / anomaly z-score targets: failed cross-site (lofo_r2 ~ -0.0006)
- Antecedent moisture + rain x surplus interactions: REG a wash, CLF only +0.017 PR-AUC
- Riparian 0-2km bucket: CLF +0.039 PR-AUC but REG worse
- Advective travel-time routing IS ALREADY IMPLEMENTED (weather per distance bucket shifted by median flow distance / 2.1 m/s) and is part of the "lagged weather hurt" failure.
PATTERN: nearly every hydrologically-motivated TEMPORAL feature has failed. The only wins came from geometry and static geography. This strongly suggests the deficit is in BETWEEN-SITE static information, not in temporal dynamics.

## Data present on disk but UNUSED
- discharge/streamflow: only 22 of 85 sites (all USGS, 0.66-0.97 density, up to 18 years). ZERO of the 61 IWQIS sites.
- co-located water chemistry: specific conductance (65 sites), water temp (80), pH (64), dissolved oxygen (64), turbidity + phosphate (61)
- upstream_uid (28 sites) / downstream_uid (40 sites) river-network topology: completely unread
- draining_area (80/85), NHDPlus comid (stored per basin), basin containment graph (used only to build CV folds)

## Known data problems
- Nitrogen surplus (gTREND product) ENDS IN 2017 -> NaN for 68% of training rows
- 16.5% of grid cells lack crop/surplus data; an inner join silently UNDER-COUNTS crop area and N surplus for basins extending outside Iowa (worst for the largest multi-state basins)
- Tile drainage density: known to be the dominant hydrologic control in Iowa, NOT in the feature set, and NO data source has been identified yet


## Non-negotiable rules for this research

1. RECORD THE SPLIT PROTOCOL FOR EVERY PERFORMANCE NUMBER, AND DO NOT COMPARE NUMBERS ACROSS PROTOCOLS. Random-split results are valid evidence about method behavior and should be reported - researchers using them often have good reasons for their own question. But only SPATIALLY HELD-OUT numbers (leave-one-basin-out, leave-one-region-out, ungauged-basin protocol) are comparable to our LOFO 0.820, because a random split over autocorrelated site-days lets a model memorize a site's level and measures interpolation rather than transfer. When the protocol cannot be determined, say so rather than guessing.
2. REPORT EFFECT SIZES AND SAMPLE SIZES, NOT CONCLUSIONS. "GNNs improve water quality prediction" is worthless. "Recurrent GCN, 456 reaches, 42 monitored, held-out-node RMSE 1.83 vs 2.11 for LSTM" is actionable. Always give the number of catchments/basins/sites used.
3. EVERY DATASET RECOMMENDATION MUST BE OPERATIONAL: exact name, spatial resolution, temporal resolution, coverage years, whether it covers ALL of Iowa AND the multi-state portions of basins, exact URL, access mechanism (API/bulk/FTP), authentication requirement, and license.
4. ACTIVELY HUNT FOR NEGATIVE RESULTS. Seven feature-engineering ablations have already failed on this project. Papers reporting that a technique did NOT transfer are as valuable as successes and are systematically under-published - look in discussion/limitations sections and in benchmark comparison papers.
5. FLAG THE n=19-FAMILIES CONSTRAINT against every recommendation. If a method's evidence base comes from 300+ basins, say so explicitly and assess whether it can work at n=19.
6. ACQUISITION CONSTRAINT: recommend only free/public data, or data obtainable by a reasonable request (e.g. emailing IIHR or Iowa DNR). No paid datasets, no field campaigns, no new sensor deployment.
7. Prefer peer-reviewed literature and authoritative agency sources over blog posts. Give DOIs where they exist.
8. JUDGE EVERYTHING AGAINST THE DEPLOYMENT TARGET: an arbitrary ungauged map pin with no local history. State plainly when a method only works at gauged sites.


## Your assignment: synthesize the findings for angle "Borrow a calibrated process model instead of learning physics: SPARROW / SWAT / Iowa NRS outputs as features"

### Research question
Which calibrated process-model outputs for nitrogen in Iowa and the Mississippi basin are publicly downloadable per NHDPlus reach or per catchment? And does injecting process-model output as an INPUT FEATURE to an ML model improve ungauged-site skill, relative to the ML model alone?

### What a good answer contains
For USGS SPARROW (especially Midwest / Mississippi-Atchafalaya total-nitrogen models): what is published, at what spatial unit, downloadable how, which vintage, incremental vs total yield, and known limits. Likewise for the Iowa Nutrient Reduction Strategy modeling, EPIC/APEX/SWAT Iowa applications, and any published gridded nitrogen-leaching product. The process-guided ML literature (Read, Jia, Karpatne): pretrain on process-model output then fine-tune on observations, and physics-informed loss terms - with reported gains and the specific conditions under which pretraining helped (usually sparse labels, which is exactly our between-site situation). A caution about CIRCULARITY if a SPARROW model was itself calibrated using some of our 85 monitoring sites.

### TIER 3 - UNVERIFIED claims
These were extracted from real sources but were NEVER adversarially verified - verification was cut to conserve budget. The characteristic failure mode in this corpus is CONFIDENT OVERREACH FROM THIN EVIDENCE, not fabrication: a claim's conclusion is often right while its stated warrant is wrong, its effect size misattributed, or its split protocol misdescribed.

STRICT RULES for tier 3, which you MUST follow:
- USE them for COVERAGE and LEADS: naming a dataset, a URL, an access route, a candidate attribute, or an angle worth pursuing.
- DO NOT use them as the warrant for any numeric performance figure, any effect size, or the core argument of any recommendation. Those must rest on verified (tier 1) claims.
- Any finding that rests on tier 3 MUST set confidence to "unverified" and say so in the claim text itself.
- If a tier 3 claim contradicts a verified claim, the verified claim wins; note the conflict.

Produce the structured finding set for this angle as JSON.

Merge semantic duplicates. Apply every correction supplied by the verifiers. Rank findings by relevance to the BETWEEN-SITE gap specifically. For each finding give feasibilityAtN19 and worksAtUngaugedPin honestly. Populate "datasets" for every concrete data source, with howToIncorporate written concretely enough to act on - name the feature that would be created and how it would be aggregated to a basin. Populate "uncovered" for any part of the question that produced nothing verifiable - absence of evidence must be reported as absence, never silently dropped. Your "verdict" must state plainly whether this angle is worth pursuing and why.

Output JSON with keys: angle, verdict, findings[] (each: claim, confidence, effectSize, splitProtocol, nBasins, sources[], feasibilityAtN19, worksAtUngaugedPin), datasets[] (each: name, url, resolution, years, access, license, coversMultiState, whyUseful, howToIncorporate, limitations), refuted[], uncovered[].
angleTitle: Borrow a calibrated process model instead of learning physics: SPARROW / SWAT / Iowa NRS outputs as features

tier1_survived.claim: The 2012 Midwest SPARROW total-nitrogen model (Robertson & Saad 2019, SIR 2019-5114, Table 5) was calibrated on TN loads from 1,334 monitoring sites (1,344 considered, 1,335 in Table 1) and reports R2 = 0.950, Yield R2 = 0.913, conditioned RMSE = 0.487 natural-log units (51.8% in real space) and unconditioned RMSE = 0.555 log units (60.0% in real space). CRITICAL CAVEAT: these are IN-SAMPLE calibration statistics from nonlinear least-squares regression; the report presents no cross-validation, no leave-one-basin-out, and no spatial holdout anywhere. The 'Yield R2 = 0.913' is therefore NOT comparable to our between_r2 = 0.21 under LOFO — it is the in-sample cross-sectional fit of a 16-parameter regression to 1,334 sites, and the honest expectation for a truly unseen basin is materially worse. The 'conditioned' RMSE (0.487) is additionally optimistic because it resets predicted accumulated loads to MEASURED loads at upstream calibration sites — that is a gauged-upstream-neighbor protocol that DOES NOT WORK for our arbitrary-map-pin deployment target. Only the unconditioned RMSE (0.555 log units / 60%) reflects prediction with no upstream measurements, which is our situation.

tier1_survived.splitProtocol: not-applicable — in-sample calibration fit only; no holdout or cross-validation reported in the entire 60-page report
tier1_survived.nBasins: 1,334 TN calibration sites (2,012 for the streamflow model; 1,273 TP; 107 suspended sediment)
corrections: The claim is correct in every material respect; only one incidental number is wrong. It describes the TN model as "a 16-parameter regression." Table 5 lists 17 model terms, of which 14 are ESTIMATED coefficients (6 source: atmospheric deposition, wastewater treatment plants, urban and open areas, fertilizers, manure, fixation; 6 land-to-water: ln runoff, detrended air temperature, ln tile drains, ln soil clay content, CRP acres, ln no-till; 2 aquatic loss: instream decay for mean streamflow <1.4 m3/s, reservoir loss). The remaining 3 are fixed or specified rather than fitted, carrying "--" for standard error, p-value and t-value: Canada load (set to 1.0), stream loss from groundwater pumping for irrigation (1.221), and surface-water withdrawal for public supply (set to 1.0). So the correct phrasing is "a 14-parameter regression (17 listed terms, 3 of them fixed)" fit to 1,334 sites. This makes the ratio of sites to estimated parameters ~95:1, which if anything sharpens the claim's own n=19 argument: our 19 independent basin families could not support this model structure at all. Two further refinements, neither contradicting the claim: (1) Table 1 also lists a fifth model, suspended solids (1,085 considered / 1,082 final), which the claim omits — no error, just incomplete. (2) The claim could state more strongly that Yield R2 = 0.913 and our between_r2 = 0.21 are not merely different PROTOCOLS but different RESPONSE VARIABLES — mean-annual TN load/yield in log space for 2012 versus daily-max nitrate concentration — so they would be non-comparable even if SPARROW had been spatially cross-validated.

The claim is accurate in every load-bearing particular; three refinements, none of which touch a reported effect size.

(a) "16-parameter regression" is wrong. Table 5 lists 17 coefficient terms, of which 3 are FIXED/specified rather than estimated (Canada load = 1.0; surface-water withdrawal for public supply = 1.0; stream loss from groundwater pumping for irrigation = 1.221 — all three show "--" for standard error, p-value, and t-value). Exactly 14 coefficients were estimated by nonlinear least squares: 6 source (atmospheric deposition 0.163, WWTP 0.495, urban/open areas 122, farm fertilizers 0.032, manure 0.066, fixation 667), 6 land-to-water (ln runoff 0.673, detrended air temperature -0.048, ln % tile drains 0.101, ln soil clay 0.292, CRP/farm-acre ratio -4.758, ln % no-till 0.124), and 2 aquatic loss (instream decay for mean flow <1.4 m3/s 0.375, reservoir loss 3.357). Say "14 estimated coefficients (17 terms, 3 fixed)".

(b) "60-page report" — the PDF is 88 pages; the main body runs to Summary and Conclusions at ~p. 55-56, followed by references and 4 appendices. The exhaustive-search conclusion holds across all 88 pages.

(c) Add two non-comparabilities BEYOND the protocol issue, so that even the unconditioned 0.555 ln-unit figure is not mistaken for a benchmark we should match. First, different target and different variance denominator: SPARROW predicts long-term mean-annual TN LOAD (kg/yr) and YIELD (kg/km2/yr) for a 2012 base year, and Yield R2 = 0.913 is a cross-sectional fit across a continental-scale domain (Dakotas to Ohio) where yields span orders of magnitude; our between_r2 = 0.21 is the absolute level of DAILY-MAX CONCENTRATION across 19 Iowa corn-belt basin families with a severely restricted between-site range. The R2 = 0.950 on loads is further inflated by drainage-area scaling, which is precisely why the report also reports the area-normalized Yield R2 (0.913) — and for the weaker constituents the same gap is much larger (suspended sediment R2 0.837 vs Yield R2 0.651; TP R2 0.875 vs Yield R2 0.741). Second, different temporal resolution: SPARROW is a steady-state annual-mean model with no time dimension whatsoever, so it says nothing about daily exceedance timing — the half of our problem the model already handles well (within_r2 0.42, macro_auc 0.90).

The claim stands on every load-bearing point and should be used as written. Three peripheral corrections, none of which affect the conclusion:

1. "16-parameter regression" is wrong. The report states: "The 2012 Midwest SPARROW TN model has 17 variables (table 5)." Of those, two coefficients were not freely estimated — the public-supply withdrawal coefficient was "directly included in the model without calibration (coefficient set to 1.0)" and the groundwater-irrigation coefficient was fixed to the streamflow model's value of 1.221 — so 17 variables with 15 freely calibrated coefficients. Say "17-variable (15 freely calibrated)" rather than "16-parameter".

2. "107 suspended sediment" calibration sites is wrong by an order of magnitude. Table 9 gives the SS model n = 1,185 sites (with conditioned RMSE 0.989 / 129%, unconditioned 1.112 / 156%, R2 0.837, Yield R2 0.651). Table 1 lists 60,360 original suspended-sediment/TSS sites and 1,262 considered.

3. Minor: the TP model's Table 7 reports n = 1,271, while Table 1 reports 1,273 "used in final SPARROW models" — cite 1,271 if quoting the TP model table. And the report is 74 p. including 5 appendixes (88 PDF pages), not 60 p.; the "no cross-validation anywhere" finding holds across the full 74 p.

One strengthening amendment: the claim says "Only the unconditioned RMSE (0.555 log units / 60%) reflects prediction with no upstream measurements, which is our situation." True, but the unconditioned RMSE is STILL an in-sample statistic — those same 1,334 sites' measured loads are what estimated the coefficients. It removes the gauged-upstream-neighbor conditioning but not the calibration-set membership. So 0.555 ln-units / 60% is a LOWER BOUND on true ungauged-basin error, not an estimate of it; the honest ungauged expectation is worse still, particularly in the report's own documented weak regions (western study area, Dakotas) and at low loads (0.65 ln-units for loads below 14 ln-units even in-sample).

corrections:
The claim stands as written; four precision fixes and three usage caveats.

PRECISION FIXES
(a) The server does NOT honor HTTP Range. There is no accept-ranges header, and a request with `-r 400000000-400002000` returned HTTP 200 with content-length 493183556 and the file from byte 0 (I got the header back, not the middle). Header verification works only because curl truncates a streamed full GET. Practical consequence: you cannot cheaply sample the middle of these files — plan on streaming and filtering (`curl ... | awk`) or a full 493 MB download.
(b) "1 row per NHDPlusV2 COMID" is right but not exactly — the file also carries a small number of negative synthetic reach ids (e.g. -92000151, -91074001) that are not NHDPlusV2 COMIDs. 18 of the first 167,893 rows. Filter comid > 0 before joining.
(c) The record lists 8 files, not 7: the seven data files plus an FGDC XML metadata file (listed with size 0 in JSON but fetchable). The XML is where the units live and should be read before deriving anything.
(d) Item-level `rights` is null. USGS data releases are public domain / CC0 by agency policy, but the release itself does not state a license string.

USAGE CAVEATS FOR THIS PROJECT
(1) The concentration derivation is NOT unit-safe as stated. al_tn is a long-term mean annual load and wbm_meanq is a mean flow whose units (kg/yr and ft3/s, most likely) are defined only in the FGDC XML — do not compute al_tn/(annual volume) until you have read the XML. Get the units right or the derived "concentration" will be off by a constant factor per reach, which is harmless for a tree split but not for interpretation.
(2) CIRCULARITY RISK, and it is the real one. SPARROW is a calibrated model, not an observation. Robertson & Saad (2019, SIR 2019-5114) calibrated the Midwest TN model against monitored load estimates at stream sites — and Iowa's monitoring network is exactly where this project's ~85 sites live. If any of the 85 sites (or their reaches) were SPARROW calibration sites, then al_tn/il_tn at those reaches encodes the observed nitrate level at the site, and a LOFO fold that holds out a basin family will still see a feature that was fit to that family's own loads. That is leakage that LOFO does not catch, because the leak is baked into the covariate rather than into the split. Before using this, pull the calibration-site list from SIR 2019-5114 and check overlap with the 85 sites; if there is overlap, report both "with SPARROW" and "with SPARROW, calibration-overlapping families dropped".
(3) It is a static 2012 base-year mean-annual product, so it can only move the between-site term. That is the correct place to aim — the project's own diagnostic (between_r2 0.21, between_rate_r2 0.24, seven failed temporal ablations, wins only from static geography) says the deficit is between-site static information. il_tn/IncAreaKm2 (incremental TN yield), the fert/man/nfix source shares, and DEL_FRAC are per-reach static scalars that describe exactly the "how loaded is this basin" quantity the model is missing, and they can be aggregated over an arbitrary NLDI-delineated basin at prediction time with no local history and no gauge — so it IS compatible with the arbitrary-map-pin deployment target. But note that with n=19 independent basin families you are adding correlated static columns to a between-site regression with ~19 effective units; expect the honest test to be whether between_rate_r2 moves at all under LOFO, and expect wide error bars on any gain. Add a small number of SPARROW-derived columns (yield, dominant source share, DEL_FRAC), not all 40.

The claim is accurate in every checkable particular — file names, all seven byte sizes, the 3.85 GB total, the exact 40-column TN header in order, no-authentication access, the URL/JSON enumeration mechanism, one unique row per COMID, and the derivability of yield and concentration. Four small corrections and one significant omission:

1. RANGE REQUESTS DO NOT WORK. The claim says the header was "verified by HTTP range request." ScienceBase ignores the Range header: `curl -r 0-3000` returns HTTP 200 with content-length 493,183,556 and no accept-ranges, downloading the full 493 MB. You must stream and truncate (`curl -s URL | head -c N`, accepting a broken pipe). Budget bandwidth accordingly — the conclusion is unaffected, the method is not.

2. THERE IS NO WORKING DATA DICTIONARY. The item lists an 8th file (the FGDC metadata XML) with size 0, and its download URL returns an HTML 404 page; `?format=xml` returns 415 and `?format=fgdc` returns a 4-byte empty response. Column units are therefore undocumented in the release. I established them empirically: al_tn/il_tn in kg/yr, wbm_meanq in cfs. Authoritative definitions live in the companion report, not the data release.

3. ATTRIBUTION SPLIT. Saad & Robertson 2020 is correct for the data release, but the model itself — construction, calibration, and any performance/validation numbers — is documented in Robertson, D.M., and Saad, D.A., 2019, USGS SIR 2019-5114, DOI 10.3133/sir20195114. Cite that for anything about model quality; the data release contains no performance number.

4. GUARD THE YIELD DIVISION. 19 rows have IncAreaKm2 == 0 (il_tn/IncAreaKm2 divides by zero), and 18 COMIDs are negative synthetic/non-NHD segments that will not join to NLDI. Both are trivial in volume (37 of 1.38M rows) but will crash a naive pipeline.

5. OMISSION, and the most valuable part of the release for this project: mw_sparrow_model_input.txt is an 89-column per-ComID attribute table that includes `tiles13_perc2` / `ltiles13_perc2` — per-catchment tile drainage percentage, the control the project brief flags as dominant in Iowa with no identified source — plus ldrainden, CAT_STCLAY, CAT_KFCTUP, CAT_ELEV, lCAT_notill, ManN2012, fert_sw_N_kg (2012 fertilizer N), cmaq_TN_12_kg, and aridity. Same free URL pattern, same COMID key, same Iowa + multi-state coverage.

Two conditions before using any of this as a feature: (i) test the calibration leakage — SPARROW is fit to monitoring-station loads, the input file's flux_600_final column identifies TN calibration reaches, so check whether any fall inside the 85 sensor basins before believing a LOFO improvement; (ii) respect n=19 — add one or two static columns (incremental TN yield, tile drainage percent), not the full attribute table.

The claim is accurate; four small corrections and additions:

1. FILE COUNT: the item exposes EIGHT file entries, not seven. The eighth is the FGDC metadata XML, listed at size 0 bytes, and its download URL returns HTTP 404. Practical consequence: there is NO attribute-level units documentation attached to the data release. Units are not stated anywhere in the CSVs. I established them empirically as kg/yr for all al_*/il_* load columns and cfs for wbm_meanq (verified by the resulting concentrations landing in the physically correct 0.4-7.6 mg/L range Midwest-wide). Anyone using this must confirm units from the model report, not the release.

2. MISSING COMPANION CITATION: the item's webLinks field points to the model documentation, which the claim omits and which is where calibration design, coefficients, and units are described: Robertson, D.M., and Saad, D.A., 2019, "Spatially referenced models of streamflow and nitrogen, phosphorus, and suspended-sediment loads in streams of the Midwestern United States," USGS Scientific Investigations Report 2019-5114, 74 p., DOI 10.3133/sir20195114. Note the author order is reversed between the report (Robertson & Saad 2019) and the data release (Saad & Robertson 2020); both are correct for their respective objects.

3. RANGE REQUESTS ARE NOT HONORED. The claim says the header was "verified by HTTP range request." The server ignores the Range header: it returns HTTP 200 with content-length 493183556, not HTTP 206 with a partial body. Any apparent success is client-side truncation, and a naive range request will pull the whole 493 MB. Immaterial to the substance, but the stated verification method does not do what it says.

4. "1 ROW PER NHDPlusV2 COMID" is 1,379,904 unique rows, of which 18 have NEGATIVE comid values (e.g. -92000151, -92000150) — SPARROW-internal synthetic reaches that will not join to NHDPlusV2. Filter comid > 0. Trivial in magnitude (18 of 1.38 M) but will otherwise produce silent join misses.

5. LICENSE: the item's rights field is null and no license file is attached. It is a USGS data release and is public domain / US Government work in practice, but the release itself asserts no explicit license string.

tier1_survived.claim: The Midwest 2012 SPARROW total-nitrogen model was calibrated on long-term mean-annual TN loads from 1,334 monitoring sites and reports in-sample fit statistics R2 = 0.950 (on log accumulated load), Yield R2 = 0.913, conditioned RMSE = 0.487 natural-log units (51.8% in real space), and unconditioned RMSE = 0.555 log units (60.0% in real space). These are CALIBRATION-FIT statistics with NO spatial holdout, no leave-one-basin-out, and no independent test set; the R2 of 0.950 is on accumulated load, a quantity dominated by drainage area, so it is not comparable to any ungauged-basin skill metric and specifically is NOT comparable to our LOFO AUC 0.820 / R2 0.328. The unconditioned RMSE of ~60% in real space is the closest thing to a transfer-relevant error and implies roughly a factor-of-1.6 typical error on predicted mean-annual load. Source: Robertson & Saad 2019, USGS SIR 2019-5114, table 5.
tier1_survived.effectSize: R2 0.950 (accumulated load, log units); Yield R2 0.913; conditioned RMSE 0.487 log units = 51.8% real space; unconditioned RMSE 0.555 log units = 60.0% real space

tier1_survived.nBasins: 1,334 TN calibration sites (Midwest region); 1,346 TN sites considered out of 93,994 water-quality sites screened
corrections: The claim is correct in substance and its central methodological conclusion is confirmed by the primary source: all four Table 5 statistics (R2 0.950, Yield R2 0.913, conditioned RMSE 0.487 log units / 51.8% real space, unconditioned RMSE 0.555 log units / 60.0% real space) are exact, and the report contains no cross-validation, no spatial holdout, and no independent test set anywhere, so these are pure in-sample calibration fit on the same 1,334 sites used to fit the 17 coefficients. Three corrections: (1) the site counts are misassigned — Table 1 gives 1,344 TN sites CONSIDERED (1,346 is the TOTAL PHOSPHORUS considered count) and 1,335 TN sites used in the final model, out of 93,994 screened water-quality sites; Table 5 and the body text say 1,334, a one-site internal inconsistency in the report itself. (2) "Factor-of-1.6 typical error" should be stated as either "a 60.0% real-space coefficient of variation" or, equivalently as a one-sigma multiplicative error, exp(0.555) = 1.74x — not 1.6x. Using unconditioned output leaks only through ~10-20 shared regression coefficients fit to 1,334 sites, where any single site carries roughly 0.07% of the calibration weight -- a weak leak, likely second-order relative to the nested-basin residual weighting. The file also contains the model's own calibration/monitoring quantities: flux_530_final, flux_154_final, flux_600_final, flux_665_final (monitored/detrended load estimates at calibration sites), mean_dflow_predpd, and the weighting terms TNAllSN_inv_resid2_hat, TPAllN_inv_resid2_hat, sedN_inv_resid2_hat, flowDN_inv_resid2_hat. Ingesting these would inject observed nitrogen load into the feature set at exactly the monitored locations, and they are unavailable in the ungauged-pin sense. The claim's named subset is safe; a blanket "ingest the file" is not.

3. VALUES ARE INCREMENTAL PER CATCHMENT, NOT BASIN-CUMULATIVE. ManN2012, fert_sw_N_kg, cmaq_TN_12_kg, sum_ptsrc_kgn_wwtp are per-catchment kilogram totals paired with IncAreaKm2. For an arbitrary map pin you must sum over the NLDI-returned upstream COMID set and then divide by CumAreaKm2 to get kg/km2 — raw sums would largely re-encode basin area, which the model already has as log_basin_area. This is mechanically compatible with the existing NLDI delineation step, so it works for the deployment target, but it is an extra accumulation stage, not a lookup.

4. TWO OF THE LISTED COLUMNS ARE NEARLY DEGENERATE IN IOWA. Measured on the downloaded file: `aridity` is exactly 0 for 99.71% of Iowa catchments (it is a western-region delivery term) and `sum_ptsrc_kgn_wwtp` is 0 for 99.10% (nonzero only where a WWTP exists — meaningful only after upstream accumulation). They cannot restore the time-varying dimension the gTREND surplus product had before 2017; they replace a 68%-NaN time series with a complete constant. That is a genuine fix for the missingness and for the between-site term, but it must not be described as recovering temporal N-input variation — it removes it.

6. THE n=19 CONSTRAINT BITES HARDEST HERE, AND THE SIR's OWN CAVEAT AMPLIFIES IT. These are static per-site features: under LOFO they take at most 19 distinct effective values, so adding ~20 of them is a ~20-parameter regression on 19 independent units. Combined with the report's county-apportionment caveat (fertilizer, manure, no-till, CRP all derive from county averages downscaled by land use), the realized between-site resolution is county-scale, which within a single Iowa basin family is close to constant. corrections:
The claim is substantively accurate and quotes the primary source almost verbatim; keep it, with five precise fixes.

1. ATTRIBUTION FIX (the only real error). The sentence "The uncertainty associated with SPARROW predictions is expected to increase for drainage basin sizes smaller than those of stream monitoring sites used to calibrate the model" is NOT in SIR 2019-5114 — the word "uncertainty" appears exactly once in the report, inside a reference title. Do not attribute it to the report. Replace it with the report's actual wording: "it is difficult to know how well the model predicted loads in drainages smaller than this... caution should be taken when interpreting the finest scale model results (for example, predictions for the individual incremental drainages of the reaches)." The quoted sentence appears to be USGS data-release/DSS boilerplate; I could not retrieve the FGDC XML for data release https://doi.org/10.5066/P93QMXC9 to confirm, so cite it as unverified or drop it.

2. THE 5 PERCENT / 31 km2 FIGURE IS TP-ONLY, AND OUR TARGET IS NITRATE. The report gives this calibration-size statistic only for the TP model. It gives no equivalent number for the TN model, whose calibration n (1,334) is close to TP's, so a similar small-basin gap is plausible but is NOT documented. Since our target is nitrate, state that the TN-model small-basin coverage is unquantified in the source rather than importing the TP number.

3. SITE-COUNT LABEL. "1,334 TN ... sites considered" is wrong; 1,334 is the TN model's final calibration n (report text and TN summary table; Table 1 says 1,335 — an internal inconsistency in the report). "Sites considered" were 1,346 TN / 1,344 TP / 1,262 SS / 2,057 streamflow; "used in final models" were 1,335 TN / 1,273 TP / 1,082 suspended solids + 107 suspended sediment / 2,012 streamflow.

4. THE SMALL-BASIN CAVEAT IS ABOUT ACCURACY, NOT AVAILABILITY — which strengthens the operational case rather than killing it. The Midwest SPARROW network has a mean catchment size of 2.7 km2 (vs 480 km2 in the 2002 models), and output is keyed to NHDPlusV2 comid, which this project already stores per basin. So a SPARROW-derived level term IS obtainable for an arbitrary NLDI-delineated map pin with no local history — it is a legitimate deployment-compatible static feature. The correct framing is: cheap to attach, but expect the feature to be least trustworthy exactly where NLDI pins land on small headwater catchments, which is likely a large share of arbitrary map pins in Iowa.

5. POINT (3) OVERREACHES SLIGHTLY. "Systematic regional bias that would propagate into any feature built from SPARROW output" is stronger than the source supports for Iowa. The report locates the large residuals in the "western part of the study area" (elsewhere identified with the Missouri and Arkansas River Basins); it does not document bias in Iowa specifically. Also, a smooth regional bias in a SPARROW feature is partly absorbable by an XGBoost model that already has lat/lon as its 2nd and 3rd most important features — so residual regional bias is a reason to expect diminished marginal value, not a reason to expect harm.

FLAGGING THE n=19 CONSTRAINT (the claim does not do this and should). Adding SPARROW yield as a static per-basin covariate is a between-site term, and between-site signal is precisely what our 19 independent basin families have to estimate. One or two extra static columns is a modest, low-risk ask at n=19 — far safer than any method whose evidence base is 300+ catchments — but LOFO over 19 folds will give a very noisy estimate of its benefit; a gain smaller than roughly 0.03-0.05 PR-AUC will not be distinguishable from fold noise. Pre-register the ablation and report per-fold spread, not just the mean. Note also that SPARROW's own calibration is on 1,334 sites with nested/clustered geometry and in-sample fit statistics; its published R2 0.950 is not evidence of transfer and must not be cited alongside our LOFO 0.820.

The claim is directionally correct on all four limitations and its headline numbers (5% of TP calibration sites below ~31 km2; 14/15/28% and 19/23/52% delivery losses) are verbatim from SIR 2019-5114. Three corrections are required. FIRST, the sentence "The uncertainty associated with SPARROW predictions is expected to increase for drainage basin sizes smaller than those of stream monitoring sites used to calibrate the model" is NOT in SIR 2019-5114 -- it is data-release metadata boilerplate and must not be quoted as report text; the report's actual wording is "it is difficult to know how well the model predicted loads in drainages smaller than this" and "caution should be taken when interpreting the finest scale model results (for example, predictions for the individual incremental drainages of the reaches)." SECOND, point (3) is overstated: the report used SPATIALLY VARYING land-to-water delivery variables in this study; only the source coefficients are spatially constant, and the large residuals persisted despite the spatially varying delivery terms. Moreover the residual problem is located in the arid WESTERN part of the study area where calibration site density is lowest, whereas Iowa is in the eastern/Corn Belt portion where site density is highest -- so the propagated-regional-bias risk for Iowa map pins is substantially smaller than the claim implies. THIRD, the site counts mix two different columns of Table 1: 1,346 TN / 1,344 TP / 1,262 SS / 2,057 streamflow were CONSIDERED; 1,334 TN (per text), 1,335 TP, 1,082+177 SS, and 2,012 streamflow were USED in final calibration. Additionally, a material fact omitted by the claim cuts in SPARROW's favor: the Midwest SPARROW input dataset already contains per-catchment tile drainage percentage (LTILES13_PERC2, from Nakagaki and Wieczorek 2016, 12 Midwest states, mean catchment 2.7 km2, joinable by NHDPlus comid) with a significant TN coefficient of +0.101 (p<0.0001) -- i.e. the data release is simultaneously a candidate source for the tile-drainage variable this project has been unable to locate. Finally, add the report's own deployment-relevant guidance, which the claim omits: USGS recommends conditioned (measurement-corrected) predictions at monitored reaches and unconditioned simulated loads only at unmonitored reaches; an arbitrary ungauged map pin can only ever receive the unconditioned, lower-accuracy prediction.

The claim is substantively accurate and the four limitations are real, correctly scoped, and quoted almost verbatim from SIR 2019-5114. Two corrections of detail:

Per report Table 1, sites CONSIDERED were 1,344 TN / 1,346 TP / 1,262 sediment / 2,057 streamflow; sites USED IN THE FINAL MODELS were 1,335 TN (text says 1,334) / 1,273 TP (text says 1,271) / 1,189 sediment / 2,012 streamflow. Three additions that strengthen the claim's practical use:

For example, for the SPARROW TP model, only 5 percent of the calibration sites were on streams with drainage areas less than about 31 km2; therefore, it is difficult to know how well the model predicted loads in drainages smaller than this. Until fine scale landscape data and monitoring data on small streams are available, caution should be taken when interpreting the finest scale model results (for example, predictions for the individual incremental drainages of the reaches).' The USGS SPARROW Midwest mapper adds that for the TN model 'the drainage areas of the smallest calibration sites are typically in the range of 10 to 100 square kilometers' and 'the uncertainty associated with SPARROW predictions is expected to increase for drainage basin sizes smaller than those of stream monitoring sites used to calibrate the model.' Also flagged: because mean catchment is ~2 km2 while 'much of the source data and landscape data used to describe variability in land-to-water delivery were derived from county-wide averages or totals' apportioned by land use, per-reach values are downscaled county statistics, not independent fine-scale measurements — so a SPARROW feature partially re-encodes county-level agricultural covariates the model may already have. Practical rule: aggregate SPARROW incremental yield over the whole delineated basin (which for our sites is large), never use a single outlet reach's incremental value, and expect the feature to be least trustworthy for map pins on headwater streams under ~30-100 km2.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: only 5% of TP calibration sites on drainages <31 km2; TN smallest calibration basins typically 10-100 km2; explicit USGS caution against using individual incremental-reach predictions
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 1,334 TN sites, of which the report only quantifies the small-basin share for TP: 5% below ~31 km2

tier3_unverified.claim: This report also closes the project's stated tile-drainage data gap, and does so twice over. The SPARROW Midwest TN model includes 'Ln (tile drains, percentage of catchment)' as a statistically significant land-to-water delivery term with coefficient 0.101, 90% CI 0.064 to 0.139, standard error 0.023, p<0.0001, t = 4.5, VIF = 2.3 — i.e. tile drainage independently increases nitrogen delivery to streams after controlling for runoff, air temperature, soil clay, CRP fraction and no-till. The underlying dataset is Nakagaki, N., and Wieczorek, M.E., 2016, 'Estimates of subsurface tile drainage extent for 12 Midwest states, 2012', USGS data release, DOI 10.5066/F7W37TDP: a 30-metre raster built from 2012 Census of Agriculture state-level tiled acreage, NLCD 2011 cultivated cropland, and STATSGO2 poorly/moderately drained soils, covering SD, NE, KS, MN, IA, MO, WI, IL, MI, IN, OH, KY — which covers Iowa AND the out-of-state portions of essentially all Iowa basins except any extending into North Dakota. Free, public domain, bulk download from ScienceBase, no authentication. EASIER PATH: it is already pre-aggregated to NHDPlusV2 catchments as field 'LTILES13_PERC2' inside mw_sparrow_model_input.txt in the SPARROW data release, so it can be joined on comid with no raster processing at all. IMPORTANT NEGATIVE / CAUTION: the sign flips by constituent — in the companion SPARROW total-PHOSPHORUS model the same tile-drain term has coefficient -0.091 (90% CI -0.156 to -0.026, p = 0.0221), which the report attributes to phosphorus sorbing to soil in tiled areas and bypassing overland flow. So tile density is not a generic 'more nutrients' proxy; the positive effect is specific to nitrogen. Also note the dataset is a downscaled state-level census estimate apportioned by soil and land cover, NOT an observed tile map, so it carries the same county-average smoothing caveat as the rest of the SPARROW inputs.
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: not-applicable — regression coefficient from in-sample calibration, no holdout reported

Outputs represent a 2012 base year for source inputs combined with long-term average hydrologic conditions for 1999-2014. CONSEQUENCE FOR THIS PROJECT: SPARROW output is a STATIC per-reach mean-annual number, not a time series. It therefore cannot contribute anything to the temporal/WHEN term (already the model's strength, within_r2 0.42) and can only act on the between-site absolute-level term (between_r2 0.21) -- which is precisely where all remaining headroom is. tier3_unverified.claim: CIRCULARITY WARNING, quantified: a spatial query of the SPARROW total-nitrogen calibration-site layer against an Iowa bounding box (-96.7, 40.3, -90.1, 43.6; envelope includes fringes of neighboring states) returns 110 calibration sites. The layer schema carries STATION_ID and STATION_NM, so overlap with this project's 85 sensor sites is directly checkable. If SPARROW per-reach output is injected as a feature, any site whose own record contributed to SPARROW's calibration has label information leaking into its own feature -- and the leakage is CONCENTRATED in the LOFO held-out fold, because leave-one-basin-family-out assumes the held-out family contributed nothing to the fitted model, which is false if SPARROW saw it. MANDATORY MITIGATION: join SPARROW STATION_ID against the 85 site identifiers, report the overlap count, and re-run LOFO with SPARROW features on the non-overlapping subset only; a gain that vanishes on the non-overlapping subset is leakage, not skill. The 61 IWQIS nitrate-sensor sites are the LOWEST circularity risk (SPARROW predates and does not typically ingest high-frequency sensor nitrate); the 22 USGS sites are the HIGHEST.

SPARROW attributes are complete across the full multi-state extent of every Iowa basin, so a SPARROW-derived nitrogen-source feature has no Iowa-boundary clipping artifact. Separately, the current nitrogen-surplus feature (gTREND) ENDS IN 2017 and is NaN for 68% of training rows; SPARROW's 2012-base-year source terms (ACCL_S1-S7) are a static, gap-free, fully-covering substitute. tier3_unverified.claim: The release is authoritative and current, and its scale means the n=19-independent-basin-families constraint does NOT bite for this data source. Full citation: Wieczorek, M.E., Jackson, S.E., Schwarz, G.E., Sekellick, A.J., and Staub, L.E., 2018, 'Select Attributes for NHDPlus Version 2.1 Reach Catchments and Modified Network Routed Upstream Watersheds for the Conterminous United States (ver. 5.0, June 2025)', U.S. Geological Survey data release, DOI 10.5066/F7765D7V. Covers approximately 2.7 MILLION NHDPlusV2 stream segments; 158 child theme items across 13 themes (Best Management Practices, Chemical, Climate and Water Balance Model, Climate, Geology, Hydrologic, Hydrologic Modifications, Landscape, Population Infrastructure, Regions, Soils, Topographic, Water use). Four linked spatial components: individual reach catchments, riparian buffer zones around reaches, catchments accumulated downstream through the network, and riparian buffers accumulated downstream. Joins via COMID (flowline ComID / catchment FEATUREID). Because these are DETERMINISTIC LOOKUPS keyed to COMID rather than statistically fitted relationships, adding them costs no effective degrees of freedom at the between-site level — unlike a method whose evidence base requires 300+ calibration basins. The n=19 constraint still applies to whether XGBoost can LEARN a stable coefficient on the new features, but not to acquiring them. As a USGS data release it is US Government public-domain / unrestricted use.
