tier3_unverified.claim: CIRCULARITY ASSESSMENT, which distinguishes two different kinds of item in this release. MOST items are SPARROW *INPUT* variables (landscape descriptors: tile drainage percent, fertilizer/manure kilograms, base flow index, soils, climate), derived from census/remote-sensing/soil sources and NOT from any nitrate observation — so joining them as ML features carries NO circularity risk with respect to the project's 85 nitrate monitoring sites. BY CONTRAST, one item IS process-model OUTPUT and carries both circularity and downscaling caveats: 'National Resource Conservation Service's Best Management Practice Scenarios for Total Non-Gas Nitrogen, Phosphorous, and Sediment' (id 5cc89237e4b09b8c0b77f247). Its own metadata states losses were simulated with APEX (Agricultural Policy Environmental Extender) per location, extrapolated to watershed scale with SWAT, under three CEAP scenarios (2003-2006 baseline, no-BMP, enhanced nutrient management), and that the index is the difference between baseline and no-implementation. Crucially it states the estimates 'were available at a large watershed (HUC2) scale, but were further processed using geospatial techniques and land characteristics to extend the information to the NHDPlus version 2.1 catchment scale' — i.e. it is HUC2-resolution information spread down to catchments, so its apparent per-catchment detail is largely interpolation artifact, and it explicitly says the index was built 'For use in the SPARROW models'. The release also contains 'Selected Conservation Practices (CPRAC) for 2012' (5d76976ee4b0c4f70d01fdcb) and NRI conservation practices 2000-2012 (5d1ceefce4b0941bde64cdea). Falsifiable: check whether the BMP index varies within a single HUC2 only as a function of land-cover weights, which would confirm it adds no genuine independent between-basin signal in Iowa.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: None reported. This release contains NO evidence on the research question of whether injecting process-model output as an ML input feature improves ungauged-site skill — that evidence must come from the process-guided ML literature (Read, Jia, Karpatne), not from this catalog.
tier3_unverified.nBasins: not-applicable

tier3_unverified.claim: SCOPE LIMIT / MOST IMPORTANT CAVEAT FOR AN UNGAUGED-PIN PRODUCT: Read et al. (2019) never tests spatial transfer. Every PGDL, DL, and process-based (PB) model in the paper is fitted to observations from the same lake it predicts; the paper states 'Our study limited the predictive challenge to a collection of lakes that were treated as independent model systems (no relationships between lakes were used or explored to improve models)' and names prediction 'in data poor or unmonitored lakes' as future work with 'parallels with predicting streamflow in unmonitored basins.' All splits are TEMPORAL holdouts within a lake. Therefore none of the paper's reported PGDL gains are evidence that process-model pretraining improves prediction at a site with ZERO local observations, which is exactly the Iowa map-pin deployment case. The paper's regime (good within-site temporal skill, per-site labels available) is analogous to the Iowa project's ALREADY-STRONG within_r2=0.42 term, not to its deficient between-site term.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Not applicable — no spatial-holdout experiment exists in this paper
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 68 lakes (multi-lake experiment) + 2 intensively studied lakes (Mendota, Sparkling); 0 spatially held out

tier3_unverified.claim: Pretraining a deep network on UNCALIBRATED process-model output and then fine-tuning on local observations beat the process model that generated the pretraining data, by a large margin. Across 68 lakes in Wisconsin/Upper Midwest (temporal holdout: test = earliest one-third of each lake's record, train = most recent two-thirds, 133 to 1,788 training dates per lake), median test RMSE was 1.65 degC for PGDL, 1.78 degC for DL, 2.03 degC for calibrated PB, and 2.78 degC for the UNCALIBRATED GLM (PB0) whose output was used as the pretraining target. Ranges: PGDL 0.91-2.66, DL 0.97-2.95, PB 1.46-3.63, PB0 1.55-4.95 degC. NEGATIVE DETAIL: PGDL was NOT better everywhere — it failed to beat 5 of 68 calibrated PB models and 5 of 68 DL models, and per-lake PB-minus-PGDL RMSE differences included negative values (as low as -0.23 degC). Relevance: shows a fine-tuned ML model can EXCEED its process-model teacher (median 2.78 -> 1.65 degC, a 1.13 degC / 41% reduction), supporting the 'inject SPARROW/SWAT output then let the ML correct it' strategy — but only where local labels exist for fine-tuning.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Median test RMSE: PGDL 1.65 vs DL 1.78 vs calibrated PB 2.03 vs uncalibrated pretrainer PB0 2.78 degC; PGDL lost to PB in 5/68 lakes and to DL in 5/68
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 68 lakes

tier3_unverified.claim: The advantage of process-guided pretraining grows as local labels get sparser, and there is a measurable crossover below which pure ML loses to the process model. On Lake Mendota (540 held-out test dates, training dates subsampled to 980/500/100/50/10/2, five random iterations), with 980 training profiles mean test RMSE was 0.92 degC (PGDL), 1.07 degC (DL), 1.56 degC (calibrated PB). Pure DL beat PB when trained on 500 profiles (1.28 vs 1.49 degC) or more, but LOST to PB at 100 profiles (1.73 vs 1.64 degC) or fewer. With only 2 training profiles, PGDL scored 1.77 degC vs PB 3.03 degC. The authors conclude 'the greatest gains of PGDL temperature modeling ... were when observations were relatively scarce' and that 'even a small number of water temperature sampling dates (e.g., 2-100)' suffices to beat both baselines. CAUTION FOR THE IOWA PROJECT: the sparse regime tested is 2-to-100 labels AT THE TARGET LAKE, never zero; this supports process-model priors for thinly-monitored sites but does not establish behavior at n=0 local labels.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: At 980 profiles PGDL 0.92 vs DL 1.07 vs PB 1.56 degC; at 2 profiles PGDL 1.77 vs PB 3.03 degC; DL-vs-PB crossover between 100 and 500 profiles
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 1 lake (Lake Mendota); parallel experiment on Sparkling Lake

tier3_unverified.claim: NEGATIVE RESULT — process-model pretraining can make the hybrid model WORSE than the process model alone if the pretraining output does not span the conditions being predicted. Read et al. re-ran Lake Mendota experiments with 'limited pretraining' (synthetic GLM output restricted to the training period only, removing 1980-2008) versus 'extended pretraining' (from April 1980 onward). When models were trained on cold-season data and asked to predict summer (seas500), limited-pretraining PGDL scored 1.98 degC RMSE versus 1.19 degC for extended pretraining — and the 1.98 degC was WORSE than the calibrated process model's 1.91 degC. With only 2 training profiles the gap was 1.77 (extended) versus 2.67 degC (limited). The limited seas500 pretraining set was under 20% the size of the extended set and 'contained no data from any summer period.' Conversely, when training data were plentiful and train/test conditions matched (sim980, sim500), reduced pretraining had 'minimal' impact, and the limited-vs-extended difference 'monotonically decreased as data [increased].' IMPLICATION: a SPARROW/SWAT feature injected into the Iowa model must produce output spanning the target basins' full condition range, or it can actively degrade skill — consistent with this project's seven prior failed temporal-feature ablations.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: seas500: limited-pretrain PGDL 1.98 vs extended-pretrain 1.19 degC, vs calibrated PB 1.91 degC (limited pretraining LOST to the process model); 2-profile case 2.67 vs 1.77 degC
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 1 lake (Lake Mendota)

tier3_unverified.claim: The physics-informed LOSS TERM contributes far less than pretraining — relevant because a physics loss is much harder to construct for nitrate than for lake energy balance. Read et al. did not ablate the two components ('we did not separately test the contributions of energy conservation and pretraining') but state 'it is likely that pretraining is responsible for the majority of predictive gains,' and that the energy-conservation penalty 'likely serves as a regularization term that improves the generalizability of the model, while pretraining acts as a powerful surrogate for real observations when comprehensive training data are limited.' They cite Jia et al. (2019) as having isolated the energy-conservation loss and found 'small but consistent improvements in accuracy when compared to an otherwise identical LSTM (although this finding was not tested for out-of-bound training data), and larger improvements when models added a pretraining step.' IMPLICATION: for the Iowa nitrate model the actionable half of the PGDL recipe is the cheap half — use calibrated process-model output as a FEATURE or pretraining target — not a bespoke physics loss.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Not separately quantified in Read et al. 2019; cited Jia et al. 2019 reports 'small but consistent' gain from the energy-conservation loss vs 'larger improvements' from pretraining
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 68 lakes (Read et al.); Jia et al. 2019 ablation basin count not reported in this paper

tier3_unverified.claim: THE ACTUAL UNGAUGED-SITE TEST IS THE COMPANION PAPER, and its effect size is far smaller than Read 2019's within-lake gains. Willard, Read, Appling, Oliver, Jia & Kumar (2021), 'Predicting Water Temperature Dynamics of Unmonitored Lakes With Meta-Transfer Learning,' WRR 57, DOI 10.1029/2021WR029579 (open access), built source models at 145 well-monitored lakes and predicted 305 target lakes TREATED AS UNMONITORED (true spatial holdout; plus an expansion to 1,882 additional target lakes). Median target-lake RMSE: uncalibrated GLM (PB0) 2.52 degC; PB-MTL 2.43 degC; PGDL-MTL 2.16 degC; ensemble of 9 PGDL sources per target 1.88 degC. So the entire meta-transfer apparatus bought 0.64 degC (25%) over simply running the uncalibrated process model at the ungauged site, versus the 1.13 degC median gain PGDL achieved at MONITORED lakes. Notably 'for sparsely monitored target lakes, PGDL-MTL often outperformed PGDL models trained on the target lakes themselves,' and the single most important transfer predictor was difference in maximum depth between source and target. n=19 CONSTRAINT FLAG: this method requires a metamodel trained on 144x145 = 20,880 source-to-source transfer pairs. With 19 independent basin families Iowa would have at most ~19x18 = 342 pairs, roughly 1.6% of that, and lake 'max depth' has no obvious nitrate analogue of comparable discriminating power — meta-transfer source selection is likely INFEASIBLE at this project's scale, though the simpler finding (uncalibrated process-model output as a baseline/feature at ungauged sites) transfers directly.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Median RMSE at ungauged targets: uncalibrated PB0 2.52 -> PB-MTL 2.43 -> PGDL-MTL 2.16 -> 9-source PGDL-MTL ensemble 1.88 degC (0.64 degC / 25% total gain over raw process model)
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 145 source lakes, 305 target lakes held out as unmonitored, plus 1,882 expanded targets

tier3_unverified.claim: Jia et al. (2021) use process-model output in TWO distinct ways in the same system, and both are directly transplantable in principle: (a) as direct INPUT FEATURES — 'Other input features (shade fraction, solar radiation, potential evapotranspiration) are difficult to measure frequently, and we use values produced by the PRMS-SNTemp model as its internal variables' (3 of their 10 input dimensions are process-model output, not observations); and (b) as PRETRAINING TARGETS — simulated intermediate physical variables (streamflow, stream temperature, relative humidity, cloud cover, groundwater and shallow subsurface flow, surface runoff) supervise the model's latent 'transferred variables' before fine-tuning on real observations. Crucially, the process model was NOT region-calibrated: 'Since a region-specific calibration PRMS-SNTemp is extremely time-consuming, a version with default values of parameters is widely used in the hydrologic domain. We provide a comparison with this version referred to as the PRMS-SNTemp model.' This falsifies the assumption that a process model must be locally calibrated to be a useful ML input — and it also eliminates circularity, since an uncalibrated model cannot have been fit to the target monitoring sites.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: 3 of 10 input features are PRMS-SNTemp internal variables; 6 simulated intermediate variables used as pretraining supervision; process model run with DEFAULT (uncalibrated) parameters
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 42 river segments (Delaware River Basin subset)

tier3_unverified.claim: The headline '33%/14% improvement over the physics-based model and 24%/14% over LSTM' from Jia et al. (2021) is measured under a TEMPORAL holdout, not a spatial one: 'we train each ML model using data from the first 24 years (Oct 01, 1980 to Sep 30, 2004) and then test in the next 12 years (Oct 01, 2004 to Sep 31, 2016)', with all models global and applied to all 42 segments. The '0.1% / 2%' sparsity is achieved by RANDOMLY SUBSAMPLING labeled site-days from the first 24 years — it is sparsity in TIME at already-monitored segments, not sparsity in SITES. This is therefore NOT the ungauged-basin regime and these numbers are not comparable to a leave-one-basin-out AUC of 0.820. Temperature RMSE at 0.1% labels: PRMS-SNTemp 3.661 (fixed), ANN 3.706±0.114, RNN 3.234±0.057, RNN-pretrained 2.818±0.059, RGrN 2.849±0.049, PGRGrN-ptr 2.556±0.045, PGRGrN-ptr+ctr 2.464±0.105.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Temp RMSE 0.1% labels: RNN 3.234 -> PGRGrN-ptr+ctr 2.464 (-23.8%); PRMS-SNTemp alone 3.661
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 42 segments; temperature observed on 32 segments (51,103 obs), streamflow on 18 segments (206,920 obs), Oct 1980-Sep 2016 (13,149 dates)

tier3_unverified.claim: The benefit of pretraining on process-model output in Jia et al. (2021) DECAYS SHARPLY as labeled data increases, and for streamflow it essentially vanishes at full label density. Temperature RMSE, RNN vs RNN-pretrained-on-simulations: 3.234 -> 2.818 at 0.1% labels (-12.9%), 1.908 -> 1.810 at 2% (-5.1%), 1.546 -> 1.444 at 100% (-6.6%). Streamflow RMSE, RNN vs RNN-pretrained: 6.885 -> 6.367 at 0.1% (-7.5%), 5.718 -> 5.529 at 2% (-3.3%), 4.406 -> 4.104 at 100% (-6.9%). Full-model comparison at 100% labels: PGRGrN-ptr+ctr 4.076 vs RNN-pretrained 4.104 — a 0.7% difference, i.e. the entire graph + contrastive-loss apparatus buys almost nothing once labels are dense. FALSIFIABLE IMPLICATION FOR THIS PROJECT: our regime is 160,074 labeled site-days (dense in time, sparse in SITES), which resembles their 100% column far more than their 0.1% column. The published condition under which process-guided pretraining paid off — extreme temporal label scarcity at monitored locations — is NOT our condition.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Pretraining gain shrinks from -12.9% (0.1% labels) to -6.6% (100% labels) for temperature; full method beats simple pretrained RNN by only 0.7% at 100% labels for streamflow (4.076 vs 4.104)
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 42 segments (32 with temp obs, 18 with flow obs)

tier3_unverified.claim: Jia et al. (2021) DO run a genuine spatially-held-out experiment, but at n=5 segments, one at a time: 'Seg A to Seg E are five river segments which have sufficient observation data... We intentionally remove the temperature or streamflow observations for a specific segment during the training period (Oct 01, 1980 to Sep 30, 2004). Then we report the prediction performance... only on this segment during the testing period.' Temperature RMSE without observations (RNN -> PGRGrN-ptr+ctr): Seg A 3.328±0.132 -> 2.501±0.037, Seg B 1.384±0.065 -> 1.205±0.016, Seg C 1.804±0.041 -> 1.589±0.040, Seg D 1.805±0.038 -> 1.297±0.017, Seg E 1.646±0.075 -> 1.345±0.041 — improvement on all 5 (-12.9% to -28.2%). Streamflow RMSE without observations: Seg A 0.879±0.063 -> 0.785±0.064, Seg B 3.493±0.112 -> 3.043±0.091, Seg C 2.151±0.094 -> 1.895±0.061, Seg D 2.711±0.114 -> 2.343±0.079, Seg E 11.828±0.073 -> 10.803±0.103. This is the closest analogue to our deployment target, and it is evidence at n=5 held-out units — comparable in scale to our n=19 basin families, so the method is NOT ruled out by our sample-size constraint on evidence-base grounds.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Temperature RMSE on unobserved segments improved 12.9%-28.2% vs RNN; streamflow 10.7%-13.6%
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 5 held-out segments, one at a time, from a 42-segment network

tier3_unverified.claim: NEGATIVE RESULT (from the same paper, Table IV and Section V-B/V-F): the river-network GRAPH component actively HURTS on the segments most like an arbitrary map pin. On held-out streamflow Seg A, RGrN scores RMSE 1.271±0.035 vs plain RNN 0.879±0.063 — the graph model is 45% WORSE. The authors' explanation: 'Seg A is a head water and has no upstream river segments. Hence, the graph convolution is not helpful for modeling Seg A. Besides, the information propagated from neighbors may not always be helpful if neighboring segments have very different streamflow patterns.' Separately: 'we can see that RGrN has much larger errors than RNN over low-flow river segments. This is because the neighboring river segments tend to have similar embeddings after graph convolution and thus the training of RGrN pays even less attention to low-flow segments.' DIRECT CONSEQUENCE FOR THIS PROJECT: the deployment target has NO guarantee of a monitored upstream neighbor, and our topology data is partial (upstream_uid on only 28 of 85 sites). The graph half of PGRGrN is the half that fails exactly in our deployment condition; the PRETRAINING half (which requires no neighbors at all) is the transferable part.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Held-out streamflow RMSE: RGrN 1.271 vs RNN 0.879 — graph convolution 45% WORSE on a headwater segment with no upstream neighbors
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 1 headwater segment (Seg A) out of 5 held-out segments in a 42-segment network

tier3_unverified.claim: Jia et al. (2021) report that pure ML can be WORSE than the uncalibrated process model under label scarcity, and that pretraining is what reverses this. At 0.1% streamflow labels, PRMS-SNTemp RMSE 6.834 beats both ANN 7.116±0.120 and RNN 6.885±0.068; only after pretraining on simulations does the ML model overtake it (RNN-pretrained 6.367, PGRGrN-ptr+ctr 5.895). Additionally the paper's own generalization test — 'we test the model performance on streamflow prediction using training data only from segments with higher average streamflows (>3 m3/s) in the first 24 years... then report the RMSE in the next 12 years for segments with lower average streamflows (<1 m3/s)' — is an explicit out-of-regime spatial transfer test, and the authors note 'the performance of RGrN becomes worse in predicting segments with lower streamflows... the graph convolution makes the extracted hidden representation more similar for neighboring segments and thus RGrN simulate streamflows with similar dynamic patterns as in high-flow segments when it is trained just using observation data from high-flow segments.' This is a documented failure mode of learning the ABSOLUTE LEVEL of an out-of-distribution basin — precisely our between-site deficit (between_r2 0.21).
tier3_unverified.effectSize: At 0.1% labels the uncalibrated process model (6.834) beats plain RNN (6.885) and ANN (7.116) on streamflow; graph model degrades on out-of-regime low-flow segments
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 42-segment network split by flow regime (>3 m3/s train, <1 m3/s test); exact counts per regime not stated

tier3_unverified.claim: The USGS 2012 SPARROW Midwest models produce simulated mean-daily streamflow plus average-annual total nitrogen, total phosphorus, and suspended-sediment loads on a modified NHDPlusV2 (1:100,000-scale) reach-and-catchment network covering the Great Lakes, Lake Winnipeg, Upper Mississippi, and Ohio River basins — an extent that fully contains Iowa AND the out-of-state portions of Iowa's multi-state basins. The Midwest network contains over 1.36 million catchments with a median catchment size of 1.4 km2 (page states typical watershed size ~2.5 km2). Falsifiable: any Iowa map pin's NLDI-delineated basin should join to SPARROW reaches by NHDPlus COMID, which the project already stores per basin.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: median catchment 1.4 km2; 1:100,000 scale NHDPlusV2
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 1,360,000+ NHDPlus catchments (model network, not calibration sites)

tier3_unverified.claim: SPARROW Midwest 2012 outputs are published as BOTH 'incremental' values (generated within the individual catchment only) and 'accumulated' values (total from all upstream sources), plus 'delivery fraction' attenuation factors to downstream targets (Gulf of America, Great Lakes, or the US/Canada border). This means a per-COMID incremental total-nitrogen yield AND an upstream-accumulated TN load are both directly available as candidate static between-site features — exactly the between-site absolute-level information the project's model lacks (between_r2 0.21 vs within_r2 0.42).
tier3_unverified.effectSize: n/a — describes available output variables, not a performance gain
tier3_unverified.nBasins: unknown

tier3_unverified.claim: The SPARROW Midwest 2012 geospatial data (model inputs, model outputs, AND calibration-site information) is released at DOI 10.5066/P93QMXC9, published 2020-01-07 by the USGS Upper Midwest Water Science Center, marked CC0 1.0 Universal (public domain, no copyright restriction), with direct download from the USGS/ScienceBase data repository and NO authentication required. This satisfies the project's free/public acquisition constraint with no request-to-agency step needed.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: license CC0 1.0; DOI 10.5066/P93QMXC9; release date 2020-01-07
tier3_unverified.nBasins: not-applicable

tier3_unverified.claim: The SPARROW Midwest 2012 models represent a SINGLE STATIC 2012 base-year condition, hydrologically normalized to long-term average conditions for 1999-2014 (streamflow simulated for 1999-2014 conditions). They therefore carry NO daily or seasonal temporal signal. Consequence for this project: SPARROW output can only enter as a time-invariant per-site static feature (like lat/lon/log_basin_area), and cannot address WHEN nitrate rises. It is, however, aligned with the project's observed pattern that only geometry and static geography have produced gains while every temporal feature has failed.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: base year 2012; hydrologic normalization period 1999-2014
tier3_unverified.nBasins: unknown

tier3_unverified.claim: The SPARROW Midwest page states explicitly that 'the uncertainty associated with SPARROW predictions is expected to increase for drainage basin sizes smaller than those of stream monitoring sites used to calibrate the model,' and that the smallest calibration sites for the nutrient and sediment models have drainage areas typically in the range of 10-100 km2 (5-50 km2 for the streamflow model). Falsifiable, deployment-relevant test: any Iowa map pin whose NLDI basin is under ~10 km2 falls below the calibration support of the TN model, so a SPARROW-derived feature should be expected to degrade — this predicts a measurable interaction between basin area and any SPARROW-feature gain in LOFO CV.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: stated qualitative increase in uncertainty below 10-100 km2; no numeric uncertainty bound given on this page
tier3_unverified.nBasins: unknown (smallest TN/TP/SS calibration sites 10-100 km2; streamflow 5-50 km2)

tier3_unverified.claim: CIRCULARITY RISK IS DIRECTLY TESTABLE, NOT SPECULATIVE: the DOI 10.5066/P93QMXC9 data release explicitly includes 'calibration site information' as a published component. Because SPARROW TN calibration loads are derived from ambient stream monitoring sites, some of this project's 85 Iowa nitrate sites (particularly the USGS-operated subset that also supplies the 22 discharge records) are plausibly among them. Falsifiable check before any use: join the released calibration-site table to the 85 site locations by coordinates/COMID; every matched site makes SPARROW output partially label-derived at that site and inflates LOFO estimates, and matched sites' SPARROW features must be treated as leakage under leave-one-basin-family-out CV. NOTE: the primary calibration documentation (Robertson and Saad 2019, SIR 2019-5114, doi:10.3133/sir20195114) returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch, so the calibration site count and model R2/RMSE for the Midwest TN model COULD NOT BE VERIFIED from this source and remain unknown.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: unknown — no calibration R2 or RMSE obtainable from the accessible pages
tier3_unverified.nBasins: unknown — calibration site count not retrievable (SIR 2019-5114 returned HTTP 403)

tier3_unverified.claim: The 2012 Midwest SPARROW total-nitrogen model (Robertson & Saad 2019, USGS SIR 2019-5114, DOI 10.3133/sir20195114) was calibrated on long-term mean-annual TN loads at 1,334 monitoring sites and reports R2 = 0.950 for loads and Yield R2 = 0.913, conditioned RMSE 0.487 ln-units (51.8% in real space) and UNCONDITIONED RMSE 0.555 ln-units (60.0% in real space). The distinction is load-bearing for our deployment target: the conditioned number resets predictions to MEASURED loads at upstream calibration sites and is therefore unavailable at an arbitrary ungauged map pin; the unconditioned 0.555 / 60% is the figure that applies to an ungauged reach. These are in-sample calibration statistics on log-space mean-annual loads (which are dominated by basin size); no spatial holdout, no leave-one-basin-out validation is reported, so 0.950 is NOT comparable to our LOFO 0.820 AUC or to any held-out ML number.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: TN: R2 0.950 loads, Yield R2 0.913, conditioned RMSE 0.487 ln (51.8%), unconditioned RMSE 0.555 ln (60.0%), mean exponentiated weighted error 1.129. Error is much worse at small loads: unconditioned RMSE 0.65 for TN loads <14 ln-units vs 0.39 for >14 ln-units. Residuals spatially correlated, Moran's I = 0.199 (p=0.0005), with systematic overprediction in the southwestern study area.
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 1,334 TN calibration sites (of 93,994 original water-quality sites; 1,346 considered). Streamflow model 2,057 of 11,575 gauges; TP 1,344 considered; SS 1,262 considered.

tier3_unverified.claim: SPARROW Midwest 2012 outputs are fully public, no-authentication bulk downloads at NHDPlusV2 catchment/reach resolution, via USGS data release Saad & Robertson (2019), DOI 10.5066/P93QMXC9 / ScienceBase item 5cbf5150e4b09b8c0b700df3. Files fetched directly over HTTPS (verified 2026-07): mw_sparrow_model_output_TN.txt (493 MB), _TP.txt (446 MB), _SS.txt (501 MB), _FLOW.txt (270 MB), plus mw_reach.zip (802 MB) and mw_cats.zip (600 MB) geospatial layers and mw_sparrow_model_input.txt (740 MB) containing every catchment-level explanatory attribute used by the model. ScienceBase rightsStatement is null (USGS public domain); item created 2019-04-23. The domain covers ~1.36 million catchments spanning the entire Mississippi River, Great Lakes and Red River of the North basins, i.e. it covers ALL of Iowa AND the out-of-state portions of our multi-state basins — which is precisely where our current CDL/N-surplus inner join under-counts. An interactive subsetting alternative (export to CSV/Excel/geospatial by state, HUC, or catchment) exists at https://sparrow.wim.usgs.gov/sparrow-midwest-2012/.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: n/a - data availability claim
tier3_unverified.nBasins: ~1.36 million NHDPlusV2 catchments; median catchment 1.4 km2, mean 2.7 km2 (vs 480 km2 mean in the older 2002 SPARROW models)

tier3_unverified.claim: The Midwest SPARROW TN model includes ln(percentage of catchment with tile drains) as a statistically significant (p<0.05) land-to-water delivery variable with a POSITIVE coefficient, derived from Nakagaki & Wieczorek (2016) subsurface tile-drainage extent for 12 Midwest States, extrapolated to NHDPlusV2 catchments by the methods of Wieczorek and others (2019), and supplemented for North/South Dakota with 2016/2012 tile-permit polygons. This directly contradicts our project's assumption that 'NO data source has been identified' for tile drainage: a catchment-level tile-drainage percentage covering all of Iowa is already sitting inside mw_sparrow_model_input.txt in the same public data release, and can be aggregated over an NLDI-delineated basin as a static between-site feature without running SPARROW at all. Note the model's TP counterpart uses the same variable with a NEGATIVE coefficient (tile drains bypass overland flow), so sign expectations differ by nutrient.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Coefficient significant at p<0.05; average coefficient of variation 0.23 across the TN land-to-water delivery variables and 0.22 across source variables. Full TN variable set: sources = atmospheric deposition, wastewater treatment plants, urban+open area, farm fertilizer, manure, fixation, Canada load; delivery = ln(runoff), detrended air temperature, ln(tile drains %), ln(soil clay %), CRP/farm-acre ratio, ln(no-till %); aquatic loss = instream decay for flows <1.4 m3/s, reservoir loss, groundwater-irrigation pumping loss (coefficient fixed at 1.221).
tier3_unverified.nBasins: Tile-drainage source layer covers 12 Midwest states, extrapolated to all ~1.36M NHDPlusV2 catchments

tier3_unverified.claim: SPARROW Midwest 2012 is a STEADY-STATE, long-term mean-annual model and the authors state explicitly that its results 'enable model results to be used to rank areas based on their typical losses of a specific constituent; however, this feature does not allow areas to be ranked during any specific year or season.' Nutrient/sediment models use a 2012 base year with loads detrended to 2012 from the 2000-14 period; the streamflow model uses 2000-14 mean precipitation minus actual evapotranspiration. The report notes dynamic season-to-season SPARROW was still only under development (Smith and others, 2016). Consequence for our project: SPARROW output can ONLY serve as a static per-basin feature (one number per site, constant across all 160,074 site-days) - it can carry no temporal signal and cannot help the within-site timing term. But that is exactly the deficit our diagnostics identify (between_r2 0.21 vs within_r2 0.42, between_rate_r2 0.24), so it targets the right term; it also means it adds effectively ~1 static column against n=19 independent basin families, so any measured gain will have wide error bars.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Temporal resolution: 1 value per catchment for the 2012 base year (nutrients/sediment) and 2000-14 mean (streamflow). Zero temporal variability.
tier3_unverified.nBasins: n/a

tier3_unverified.claim: CIRCULARITY WARNING, CONFIRMED FOR IOWA: the SPARROW TN calibration loads were assembled from 71 Federal, State, regional, local, Tribal, university and private agencies, and Appendix 3 of SIR 2019-5114 explicitly lists five Iowa contributors - Iowa Department of Natural Resources (IA DNR), Des Moines Water Works (IA DMWW), Iowa Geological Survey Watershed Snapshots (IA GSWSP), Des Moines River Water Quality Network (IA ISUCOE), and Iowa Volunteer Water Monitoring Program (IA VWMP). Some of our 85 Iowa nitrate sensor sites are therefore plausibly among the 1,334 TN calibration targets, meaning SPARROW-predicted TN yield at those reaches is partly fit TO our own observations. Any measured LOFO improvement from injecting SPARROW yield as a feature is optimistically biased at held-out families whose outlets were SPARROW calibration sites. Mitigating detail: the SPARROW site-inclusion screen required >=3 years of record, >=24 samples, >=3 samples in each of four 3-month seasons, a period of record within 3 years of 2012, and a paired streamgage within 40 km with basin-area ratio 0.75-1.33 - criteria that many IWQIS continuous-sensor sites (61 of our 85, no discharge gauge) would fail. The overlap must be measured, not assumed: cross-check our site COMIDs against the calibration-site table in the data release before reporting any gain.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Unquantified overlap - requires COMID join against the data release to determine how many of our 85 sites are SPARROW calibration targets.
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 1,334 TN calibration sites drawn from 71 agencies; 5 of the listed agencies are Iowa organizations

tier3_unverified.claim: The authors caution against using SPARROW at exactly the finest spatial scale: 'most of the sites used to calibrate the SPARROW models were located on medium to large streams and may not represent the smallest streams in the Midwest. For example, for the SPARROW TP model, only 5 percent of the calibration sites were on streams with drainage areas less than about 31 km2 ... caution should be taken when interpreting the finest scale model results (for example, predictions for the individual incremental drainages of the reaches).' They further note that although catchments are ~2 km2, 'much of the source data and landscape data used to describe variability in land-to-water delivery were derived from county-wide averages or totals' apportioned by fine-scale land use - so the apparent 1.4 km2 resolution is partly downscaled county data and does not represent genuine sub-county information. For our arbitrary-map-pin product this means SPARROW-derived features are trustworthy for the accumulated/total-yield value at a reasonably sized delineated basin, but a per-cell incremental SPARROW yield used as a distance-bucket feature would be over-interpreting the product. They also warn against using calibrated SPARROW to predict the effect of adjusting individual land-to-water delivery variables, because correlated delivery variables cause omission and coefficient blending.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: 5% of TP calibration sites below ~31 km2 drainage area; unconditioned TN RMSE degrades from 0.39 (loads >14 ln-units) to 0.65 (loads <14 ln-units) ln-units, i.e. small-basin predictions are ~1.7x worse in log-error terms.
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 1,344 TP sites considered / 1,334 TN sites used; only ~5% of TP calibration sites had drainage area <31 km2

tier3_unverified.claim: Read et al. (2019) never held out a waterbody spatially. In Experiment 3, 68 lakes each got their OWN model, trained on that lake's own temperature observations (the most recent two thirds of its record) and tested on the earliest one third of that same lake's record; lakes needed at least 200 unique observation dates to be included. The authors state as an explicit limitation: 'Our study limited the predictive challenge to a collection of lakes that were treated as independent model systems (no relationships between lakes were used or explored to improve models) ... Future work could rely on the high degree of physical coherence across lakes to share information and improve models in data poor or unmonitored lakes. Given the importance of interconnections in water resources modeling, this research avenue is an important next step and has parallels with predicting streamflow in unmonitored basins.' CONSEQUENCE: this paper provides NO evidence that process-model pretraining improves prediction at a site with zero local observations, which is exactly the deployment target. Its gains are within-site temporal-transfer gains, i.e. on the 'timer' axis where the project already scores within_r2 0.42, not on the between-site absolute-level axis where the headroom is.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: n/a - protocol claim
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 68 lakes, each modeled independently; 2 lakes (Mendota, Sparkling) for the detailed experiments

tier3_unverified.claim: Experiment 3, 68 lakes, per-lake temporal holdout (test = earliest one third of each lake's record; training records ranged 133 to 1,788 unique observation dates): median test RMSE was 1.65 degC for PGDL (process-guided deep learning), 1.78 degC for DL (plain LSTM), 2.03 degC for calibrated process-based GLM (PB), and 2.78 degC for the UNCALIBRATED GLM (PB_0) whose output was the pretraining signal. Ranges across lakes: PGDL 0.91-2.66, DL 0.97-2.95, PB 1.46-3.63, PB_0 1.55-4.95 degC. The hybrid beat the plain LSTM by only 0.13 degC median (7%) while beating the raw uncalibrated process model by 1.13 degC. Per-lake, PGDL minus PB ranged from -0.23 to +2.01 degC and DL minus PGDL from -0.28 to +1.15 degC (positive = PGDL better), i.e. the hybrid LOST to the calibrated process model on some lakes and to the plain LSTM on some lakes. Relative to its pretrainer PB_0: 11 lakes improved by more than 2 degC, 55 improved by smaller amounts, and 2 lakes ended within +/-0.05 degC of the pretrainer (no gain).
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Median test RMSE PGDL 1.65, DL 1.78, PB 2.03, uncalibrated PB_0 2.78 degC. PGDL-vs-DL = 0.13 degC (7%) median. Per-lake PGDL-vs-PB range -0.23 to +2.01 degC.
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: temporal-holdout (per-lake; earliest one-third of each lake's own record held out)
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 68 lakes

tier3_unverified.claim: The benefit of process-model pretraining is a SPARSE-LABEL benefit that vanishes when labels are plentiful. Experiment 1 (Lake Mendota alone, 540 held-out test dates, RMSE averaged over five train/test iterations): at 980 training profiles PGDL 0.92, DL 1.07, PB 1.56 degC - the plain LSTM already within 0.15 degC of the hybrid. At 500 profiles DL 1.28 vs PB 1.49 degC (DL wins). At 100 profiles DL 1.73 vs PB 1.64 degC - the plain LSTM has now LOST to the process model. At only 2 training profiles PGDL 1.77 vs PB 3.03 degC (DL was not run at 2 profiles). The authors: 'the greatest gains of PGDL temperature modeling (when compared to process-based models or more traditional formulations of DL) were when observations were relatively scarce.' RELEVANCE: our label situation is 160,074 labeled site-days, i.e. the label-RICH end of this curve where the paper's own data show the hybrid advantage collapsing toward zero. Our scarcity is in INDEPENDENT SITES (19 basin families), not in labeled rows, and this paper does not test scarcity along that axis at all.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: At 980 profiles PGDL 0.92 vs DL 1.07 vs PB 1.56 degC (hybrid-over-DL gain 0.15 degC). At 2 profiles PGDL 1.77 vs PB 3.03 degC. DL beat PB at 500 profiles (1.28 vs 1.49) but lost at 100 (1.73 vs 1.64).
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: temporal-holdout (540 held-out test dates at the same lake; sparser training sets made by randomly removing whole sampling dates, five iterations)
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 1 lake (Lake Mendota)

tier3_unverified.claim: The gains come almost entirely from PRETRAINING, not from the physics-informed loss term. Read et al. state: 'Although we did not separately test the contributions of energy conservation and pretraining to improvements in predictive accuracy, it is likely that pretraining is responsible for the majority of predictive gains. Jia et al. (2019) isolated the effects of the energy conservation loss term and found small but consistent improvements in accuracy when compared to an otherwise identical LSTM (although this finding was not tested for out-of-bound training data), and larger improvements when models added a pretraining step. As such, the energy conservation penalty likely serves as a regularization term ... while pretraining acts as a powerful surrogate for real observations when comprehensive training data are limited.' CONSEQUENCE: the transferable idea for this project is 'initialize/pretrain on process-model output', not 'add a physics penalty to the loss'. But pretraining as implemented is a sequence-network weight warm-start (LSTM, 20 hidden units, Adam lr 0.005, 400 epochs) and does NOT port to XGBoost. The XGBoost-compatible analogue is injecting process-model output as an INPUT FEATURE or as a base_margin offset - a variant this paper never tests.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Energy-conservation loss alone: 'small but consistent improvements' (magnitude not quantified here, attributed to Jia et al. 2019); pretraining held responsible for 'the majority of predictive gains'.
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 68 lakes (Exp 3) plus 2 detailed lakes; the isolation experiment cited is Jia et al. 2019, on 2 lakes

tier3_unverified.claim: Pretraining on process-model output ACTIVELY HURT when the simulated data did not span the conditions of the test period - a quantified negative result. Experiment 4 (Lake Mendota) contrasted 'extended' pretraining (uncalibrated GLM output from April 1980 onward, 29 summers) against 'limited' pretraining (simulated data covering only the training period, under 20% the size, containing NO data from any summer). Predicting held-out SUMMER temperatures with 500 training profiles: extended 1.19 vs limited 1.98 degC RMSE. At that point the limited-pretrained hybrid was WORSE than the calibrated process model alone (1.98 vs 1.91 degC) - pretraining on an unrepresentative simulation made the ML model worse than the process model it was meant to improve on. With 2 training profiles: extended 1.77 vs limited 2.67 degC. Warm-years challenge at 500 profiles: extended 0.99 vs limited 1.16 degC. Authors: 'it was critical to expose PGDL to pretraining data that contained similar conditions to those found in the test period.' The limited-vs-extended gap shrank monotonically as real training data increased. RELEVANCE: a process-model feature that does not cover our prediction domain - e.g. the N-surplus layer that ENDS IN 2017 and leaves 68% of rows NaN, or a SPARROW vintage calibrated on a different era - is exactly the 'limited pretraining' failure mode quantified here, and it degraded performance below the no-ML baseline.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Held-out summers, 500 training profiles: extended pretraining 1.19 vs limited 1.98 degC RMSE (0.79 degC penalty), limited case worse than calibrated PB at 1.91 degC. 2 training profiles: 1.77 vs 2.67 degC. Warm years, 500 profiles: 0.99 vs 1.16 degC.
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: temporal-holdout, out-of-bound by design (held-out summers; held-out three warmest years 2012/2016/2017)
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 1 lake (Lake Mendota)

tier3_unverified.claim: Read et al. deliberately avoided circularity by pretraining on an UNCALIBRATED process model. Pretraining labels came from GLM v2 runs 'configured with observable lake-specific parameters (e.g., water clarity and lake depth) and driven with meteorological data from 1980 to 2018, and neither the model nor any lake-specific parameters were altered in response to performance relative to temperature observations' (PB_0). The separately calibrated GLM (PB) used as the comparison baseline was tuned on observations and was NOT the pretrainer. Pretraining data were further truncated to remove the entire test period and all dates preceding it. The authors flag as unresolved 'assessing data accuracy impacts (e.g., using calibrated instead of uncalibrated models for pretraining)' and note 'although it was clear that the uncalibrated process models used in pretraining varied in how well they represented temperature dynamics, evaluating the impact of pretrainer model quality on PGDL predictions was beyond the scope of this paper', quoting Shen et al. (2018): 'The extent to which errors in [PB] model results affect DL outcomes remains to be explored.' CONSEQUENCE FOR THE SPARROW/INRS PLAN: SPARROW total-nitrogen models ARE calibrated against monitoring records, so if any of our 85 Iowa nitrate sites (or their loads) entered a SPARROW calibration set, a SPARROW-derived feature leaks observed level information into held-out basins and would inflate LOFO scores without improving true ungauged skill. This paper supplies the clean protocol for avoiding that - use uncalibrated or independently-parameterized process output - but explicitly leaves the effect of pretrainer quality untested.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Uncalibrated pretrainer PB_0 median RMSE 2.78 degC (range 1.55-4.95) improved to PGDL median 1.65 degC after fine-tuning on observations - the fine-tuned hybrid substantially exceeded the accuracy of its own pretrainer.
tier3_unverified.splitProtocol: temporal-holdout; pretraining data explicitly masked to exclude the test period and all preceding dates
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 68 lakes

tier3_unverified.claim: Saad et al. (2019, USGS SIR 2019-5069, DOI 10.3133/sir20195069) is a CALIBRATION-TARGET dataset, not a reach-mapped model output: it publishes long-term mean daily streamflow and detrended long-term mean annual total nitrogen, total phosphorus, and suspended-sediment loads at DISCRETE MONITORING-SITE POINT LOCATIONS only. The full input/output files are in the companion USGS data release Saad, Argue, Schwarz, Anning, Ator, Hoos, Preston, Robertson and Wise (2019), 'Water-quality and streamflow datasets used for estimating long-term mean daily streamflow and annual loads to be used in regional nutrient, suspended sediment and streamflow SPARROW models, 1999-2014', DOI 10.5066/F7DN436B, free bulk download from USGS ScienceBase, no authentication, USGS public-domain license. FALSIFIABLE/DEPLOYMENT CONSEQUENCE: because values exist only at ~3,300 gauged/monitored points nationally, this release CANNOT be joined to an arbitrary ungauged Iowa map pin; it is usable only as (a) an auxiliary label set at sites that happen to be monitored, or (b) an input to the separate reach-level SPARROW model output.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Midwest funnel for nutrients: 93,994 sites with nutrient stream water-quality data -> 3,137 meeting minimum screening -> 1,470 matched to a USGS streamgage -> 1,344 TN load sites and 1,346 TP load sites considered for SPARROW (Table 3)
tier3_unverified.nBasins: ~5,200 streamflow sites, ~3,000 sediment sites, ~3,300 nutrient sites nationally; Midwest region 2,057 streamflow sites and 1,344 total-nitrogen load sites

tier3_unverified.claim: CIRCULARITY WARNING, directly checkable: the appendix agency list of SIR 2019-5069 shows that five Iowa data providers contributed water-quality data to the SPARROW load-estimation dataset — 'IA DMWW: Des Moines Water Works, Iowa', 'IA DNR: Iowa Department of Natural Resources', 'IA GSWSP: Iowa Geological Survey Watershed Snapshots', 'IA ISUCOE: Iowa State University, Des Moines River Water Quality Network', and 'IA VWMP: Iowa Volunteer Water Monitoring Program', among 137 contributing agencies. Therefore some of the 85 Iowa nitrate sites in this project (particularly the Iowa DNR / IWQIS-affiliated ones) are plausibly among the 1,344 Midwest total-nitrogen calibration targets used to fit the 2012 Midwest SPARROW model. Any use of SPARROW TN yield as an ML input feature must first cross-check site identifiers/coordinates against the DOI 10.5066/F7DN436B site table, or the leave-one-basin-family-out protocol is silently contaminated by information derived from held-out sites' own observations.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: unquantified overlap; requires direct site-ID join to measure
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 137 contributing agencies nationally; 5 Iowa-specific agencies identified; 1,344 Midwest TN calibration sites at risk of overlap with this project's 85 sites

tier3_unverified.claim: The SPARROW load estimates are STRICTLY STATIC per site: they are long-term mean ANNUAL loads computed over the 15-year window October 1, 1999 to September 30, 2014, statistically detrended by pivoting the load estimate around a base year of 2012 (specifically June 30, 2012, i.e. 2012.5) so that they represent '2012 conditions normalized to long-term average hydrology'. Streamflow was NOT detrended because the authors judged the 15-year record 'too short for detrending streamflow' (they state 20+ years is needed); only concentrations were detrended. FALSIFIABLE CONSEQUENCE for this project: a SPARROW-derived feature carries ZERO within-site temporal signal (one number per basin for all 160,074 site-days) and can therefore only ever help the between-site term — which is exactly where this project's deficit lies (within_r2 0.42 vs between_r2 0.21), but it also means it cannot be validated by any temporal ablation and adds exactly one degree of freedom against n=19 independent basin families.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: 1 static value per basin; period of record 1999-10-01 to 2014-09-30; base year 2012
tier3_unverified.nBasins: n/a (site-level static attribute)

tier3_unverified.claim: The published SPARROW calibration loads carry large stated uncertainty even after quality screening: a load estimate was retained only if its standard error was within 50 percent of the mean load estimate ('Standard errors within 50 percent of the mean load estimate were considered acceptable'), and for sites with a significant load trend, the bias ratio R had to fall between 0.66 and 1.5 (a trend-adjusted range m/1.5 to m*1.5). Sites with poor precision or large bias were excluded. FALSIFIABLE CONSEQUENCE: any per-basin SPARROW TN feature inherits an error floor of order +/-50% on the underlying observed load targets, so a downstream ML gain smaller than that noise band should not be attributed to real process information.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: retention threshold: standard error < 0.5 of mean load; acceptable bias ratio 0.66 to 1.5
tier3_unverified.nBasins: applies to all 3,300 nutrient sites; Midwest 1,344 TN sites

tier3_unverified.claim: Small ungauged headwater catchments are systematically UNDER-REPRESENTED in the SPARROW calibration set by construction. Minimum water-quality requirements were: >=3 years of record, >=24 samples, >=3 samples in each of four seasons, and a period of record within 2 years of the 2012 base year. Each water-quality site additionally had to be matched to a USGS streamgage with >=10 years of gap-free daily flow including 2012, with watershed-area ratio between 0.75 and 1.33 and aerial distance <=40 km (the area-ratio rule was relaxed only for water-quality sites with watershed area < 260 km2, which could use a nearby stream). In the Midwest this streamgage-matching step alone eliminated 53 percent of otherwise-qualifying sites (3,137 -> 1,470). FALSIFIABLE CONSEQUENCE: SPARROW's Midwest TN calibration density is biased toward larger gauged basins, so a SPARROW-derived feature is least reliable exactly for the small ungauged map pins that are this project's deployment target.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: 53% attrition (3,137 to 1,470) at the streamgage-matching step in the Midwest region; area-ratio window 0.75-1.33; max gage distance 40 km
tier3_unverified.nBasins: Midwest: 3,137 screened -> 1,470 gauge-matched -> 1,344 TN sites

tier3_unverified.claim: The reach-mapped product this project would actually need is the COMPANION release, not SIR 2019-5069: the 2012 Midwest SPARROW models (Robertson and Saad, USGS SIR 2019-5114) predict onto a digital stream network based on NHDPlus version 2 (Moore and Dewald, 2016), covering the Great Lakes, Lake Winnipeg, and Upper Mississippi and Ohio River Basins (which contains all of Iowa AND the multi-state upstream portions of Iowa basins), at a mean incremental catchment size of about 2.5 km2, and exposes incremental load/yield, accumulated load, delivered incremental load, delivered accumulated load, and concentration (mg/L). Data release: Saad and Robertson (2019), DOI 10.5066/P93QMXC9, free ScienceBase bulk download, no authentication, USGS public domain; interactive mapper at apps.usgs.gov/sparrow/sparrow-midwest-2012. UNVERIFIED IN THIS SOURCE: SIR 2019-5069 does not report the Midwest TN model's R2, RMSE, reach count, or any held-out validation, and the mapper page does not state them either; those must be read from SIR 2019-5114 itself.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: mean incremental catchment ~2.5 km2 on NHDPlusV2; model fit statistics unknown from accessible sources
tier3_unverified.nBasins: unknown (reach count not stated in accessible sources); calibrated against 1,344 Midwest TN load sites per SIR 2019-5069 Table 3

tier3_unverified.claim: The Iowa Nutrient Reduction Strategy (2013) does NOT use a calibrated process model (not SWAT, not SPARROW, not EPIC/APEX) to estimate the statewide nitrate baseline. It uses a GIS spreadsheet approach: 'Nitrate-N contribution was estimated as a function of land use and nitrogen application rates across Iowa on the basis of universal nitrogen curves (e.g. the Lawlor et al. curve...) for continuous corn and corn-bean rotations that relate subsurface flow nitrate-N concentration to nitrogen application rate. Nitrate yield is the product of nitrate concentration and water yield.' Critically, all results are reported at the MLRA (Major Land Resource Area) scale, and Iowa contains only EIGHT MLRAs ('two of the eight MLRAs have average estimates lower than optimum'). There is NO per-NHDPlus-reach and NO per-catchment output. This falsifies the core premise of the research angle for this particular source: NRS output cannot be joined to an arbitrary delineated basin as anything finer than an 8-category regional lookup, which is near-collinear with the lat/lon features the model already ranks 2nd and 3rd in permutation importance.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Spatial resolution of published output = 8 regions for the entire state
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 8 MLRAs (statewide reporting units); 0 per-reach units

tier3_unverified.claim: CIRCULARITY WARNING, directly applicable to this project: the Iowa NRS nitrate model was validated against Iowa monitoring stations that very likely overlap the project's 85 sensor sites. 'Iowa STORET and USGS stream gauge data were assembled for 26 sample stations on Iowa rivers having at least 5 years of at least monthly nitrate concentration data and a flow-weighted-average (FWA) nitrate-N concentration was calculated for each site.' Predicted concentrations 'overestimated the observed nitrate concentrations by about 17% on the basis of a least-squares statistical analysis,' with a reported 'prediction efficiency = 82.5%' for the 26 watersheds after adjusting GIS concentrations down by 17%. This 82.5% is an IN-SAMPLE fit with no held-out basins whatsoever — the 17% correction was itself estimated from the same 26 sites — so it is NOT comparable to the project's LOFO AUC 0.820, and any NRS-derived feature injected into the ML model would carry label information from sites in the training set.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: prediction efficiency 82.5%; systematic +17% overestimate of flow-weighted-average nitrate-N
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 26 Iowa river watersheds

tier3_unverified.claim: The NRS water-yield submodel is a LONG-TERM AVERAGE product with no daily resolution, so any NRS-derived quantity can only enter this project as a static per-basin feature, never as a temporal one. Method: annual water yield regressed on current and prior-year precipitation (WY_t = b1*P_t + b2*P_t^2 + b3*P_(t-1)) using 'discharge data...for 38 gauge stations distributed across Iowa' and 231 Iowa plus 127 surrounding-state weather stations (358 total), 1981–2010. 'The regression model R2 for fitting these 30 years of water yield ranged from 0.617 to 0.934 across the 38 watersheds (average 0.845).' Output was kriged to 'a 300 m water yield grid for the state of Iowa,' then 'the 1981-2010 average water yield was used' and aggregated per MLRA. Note the source weather station record was 'approximately 30% incomplete' and gap-filled by inverse-distance weighting of the 5 nearest stations. This aligns with the project's own pattern that static geography helps and temporal hydrologic features fail.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: annual water-yield R2 0.617–0.934, mean 0.845; 300 m grid; 1981–2010 climatology only
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 38 gauged Iowa watersheds (water-yield regression); 358 weather stations

tier3_unverified.claim: As of the 2013 science assessment, the Iowa NRS had NEVER been reconciled with USGS SPARROW: 'Integration and comparison to USGS SPARROW modeling' is listed explicitly in the document's own research-gaps section, alongside 'Large scale modeling to estimate nitrate-N transport with models like the Root Zone Water Quality Model (RZWQM).' SPARROW appears in the NRS only once substantively, and only for phosphorus from pasture ('nationally P loads from pastured areas are approximately 18% lower than cropland'). Consequence for this project: the two candidate process-model feature sources for Iowa nitrogen (NRS and SPARROW Midwest) are independent, mutually unvalidated products, and this document provides NO evidence that either improves prediction at ungauged sites. The USGS Midwest 2012 SPARROW data release (DOI 10.5066/P93QMXC9, CC0 1.0 public domain, NHDPlus reach/catchment units, long-term mean annual, base year 2012 for sources and 1999–2014 hydrology) is the separately downloadable per-reach product, but its TN calibration-site count and R2 could not be confirmed — pubs.usgs.gov returned HTTP 403 for SIR 2019-5114.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: not-applicable — gap statement, no performance number reported
tier3_unverified.nBasins: unknown

tier3_unverified.claim: The NRS itself flags that MLRA-scale nitrogen inputs are too coarse to represent real between-site variation — the exact failure mode this project is trying to fix. 'While MLRA scale estimates for nitrogen application rates were used in this assessment, county-based estimates from David et al. (2010) show some counties with estimated average application rates much higher than the statewide or MLRA average rate. This in part could be due to manure application rate in these counties.' The document also concedes its rates are 'based on possibly outdated data' (Blackmer et al. 1997) and that continuous-corn vs corn-soybean partitioning was a pure assumption: 'assuming continuous corn received 56 kg/ha (50 lbs/ac) more N than corn in a corn-soybean rotation... This assumption was made in the absence of actual application rate data.' Iowa total average N application rate is given as 149 kg/ha. The closing section states the aggregation problem outright: 'the practices and existing conditions were aggregated on a MLRA scale, but actual implementation would be at a much finer-scale.' This is evidence AGAINST the NRS N-input layer adding between-site signal beyond the project's existing county/gridded N-surplus features.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Iowa average N rate 149 kg/ha; continuous corn assumed +56 kg/ha (50 lb/ac); county rates 'much higher' than MLRA average
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 8 MLRAs vs 99 Iowa counties

tier3_unverified.claim: The NRS supplies two hard physical priors usable as fixed model assumptions rather than learned parameters, both stated as statewide constants: (a) flow partitioning — 'For nitrate-N load calculations the surface runoff component of the water yield was estimated to be 17% and the remaining 83% was estimated to be subsurface flow,' with 'The surface runoff nitrate-N concentration was assumed to be negligible (<1 mg/L)'; and (b) source apportionment — 'Nonpoint sources account for 92% of the total nitrogen (TN) and 80% of the total phosphorus (TP) entering Iowa streams annually,' while wastewater plants contribute 'approximately 8% of the total nitrogen,' and 'only 5% of all nitrogen inputs and 4% of all phosphorus inputs in watersheds are lost to Iowa streams' (Libra et al., 2004). Mechanistic consequence for the project's dead precipitation features: the NRS asserts that in tile-drained landscapes 'surface runoff generally has low nitrate concentration... and thus surface runoff during rain events will dilute the higher in-stream concentrations generally observed between rain events' — i.e. rainfall has a DILUTING (negative) same-day effect competing with a delayed tile-flushing (positive) effect, which is a documented mechanistic reason why a same-day scalar precipitation feature would carry near-zero net permutation importance, as observed (precip_in_1d perm ~0.000). The nonpoint reduction target is 41% of statewide total nitrogen, and full-implementation scenarios reduce load by ~127,000 tons/year, implying a baseline of roughly 310,000 tons nitrate-N/year.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: 17% surface / 83% subsurface water yield; surface runoff nitrate <1 mg/L; nonpoint 92% of TN, point 8%; only 5% of N inputs reach streams; 41% nonpoint N reduction target; ~127,000 tons/yr reduction on ~310,000 tons/yr baseline
tier3_unverified.nBasins: statewide (Iowa); constants not spatially resolved

tier3_unverified.claim: Pretraining an LSTM on the output of an UNCALIBRATED process-based model (GLM/"PB0") and then fine-tuning on observations ("PGDL") produced source models that transferred to unmonitored lakes better than transferring calibrated process-based models themselves: median RMSE over 305 held-out lakes was 2.16 C for PGDL-MTL vs 2.42 C for PB-MTL vs 2.52 C for the uncalibrated process model PB0 alone. This is direct evidence for the "borrow a process model as supervision/feature" angle: the process model's value came NOT from its own accuracy (it was the worst of the three) but from being a free source of dense pseudo-labels at every site, including sites with no observations. Note the process model must be RUNNABLE at the arbitrary target site from static attributes + weather alone -- which is exactly the property SPARROW/SWAT reach-level output would need to have for the analogous Iowa nitrate application.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: PGDL-MTL 2.16 C vs PB0 2.52 C median RMSE = 14% error reduction; PB-MTL 2.42 C = 4% reduction
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 145 source lakes, 305 target lakes treated as fully unmonitored (target observations used ONLY for final evaluation, never for training or source selection)

tier3_unverified.claim: Process-model OUTPUT was also used directly as an input feature to the meta-learner, not just as pretraining data: "GLM stratification percentage" (a statistic computed from the uncalibrated PB0 simulation at the target site) was the 2nd most important meta-feature in PB-MTL and was retained with lesser importance in PGDL-MTL. The top meta-feature in BOTH metamodels was source-target difference in maximum depth, with surface-area difference retained but less important -- i.e. the winning signals were STATIC PHYSICAL ATTRIBUTES plus a simulated-physics summary statistic, not temporal drivers. Candidate pool was 96 meta-features in four categories (lake attributes, PB0 simulation statistics, source-observation quality/quantity statistics, source-vs-target input-data distribution differences), reduced by recursive feature elimination with cross-validation (RFECV).
tier3_unverified.effectSize: not quantified per-feature beyond importance ranking; 96 candidate meta-features reduced by RFECV
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 145 source lakes

tier3_unverified.claim: The meta-learner is a gradient boosting regression that predicts source-to-target transfer RMSE, and its training set is every ordered source-source pair: 145 * 144 = 20,880 rows. THIS IS THE CRITICAL FEASIBILITY CONSTRAINT FOR THE 19-BASIN-FAMILY PROJECT. At n=19 independent families the analogous meta-training set is 19*18 = 342 pairs drawn from only 19 distinct source models and 19 distinct attribute vectors, roughly 1.6% of Willard et al.'s pair count and 13% of their distinct-source diversity. The metamodel here also learned only a weak ranking: median Spearman rank correlation between predicted and actual source-to-target RMSE was 0.659 (PB-MTL) and 0.663 (PGDL-MTL), with median meta-RMSE (error of the predicted RMSE) of 0.853 C and 0.871 C. Achieving even that weak ranking at n=19 should be treated as unproven.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: Spearman rs 0.659 (PB-MTL) / 0.663 (PGDL-MTL); meta-RMSE 0.853 C / 0.871 C
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 145 source lakes generating 20,880 source-target training pairs; evaluated on 305 targets

tier3_unverified.claim: NEGATIVE RESULT / harm rate: model transfer to unmonitored lakes made predictions WORSE than the uncalibrated process model for a large minority of targets. PB-MTL beat PB0 for only 203 of 305 lakes (33% harmed), PGDL-MTL for 226 of 305 (26% harmed), and the 9-source ensemble PGDL-MTL9 for 260 of 305 (15% harmed). Improvement magnitude increased with PB0 error, meaning transfer helped mainly where the process model was already bad and could hurt where it was good. Skill was also strongly regime-dependent: stratified target lakes had mean RMSE 2.62 C (SD 0.96, n=184) vs mixed lakes 2.01 C (SD 0.52, n=121) -- a physical-regime split analogous to a tile-drained vs non-tile-drained Iowa basin split.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: transfer degraded performance vs PB0 for 33% / 26% / 15% of targets under PB-MTL / PGDL-MTL / PGDL-MTL9
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 305 target lakes (184 stratified, 121 mixed)

tier3_unverified.claim: Ensembling multiple selected source models gave a LARGER gain than the choice of source-model type: averaging the top 9 metamodel-ranked PGDL sources (PGDL-MTL9) reached median RMSE 1.88 C vs 2.16 C for the single best-predicted source, a 13% reduction, and validation showed ensemble size mattered little between 5 and 10 sources (across the top 9 ranks the spread was only 0.09 C in median RMSE, 0.12 C in lower-quartile, 0.13 C in upper-quartile). Separately, an ORACLE that always picked the truly best available source would have scored 1.54 C (PGDL) / 1.79 C (PB), so the metamodel's source-selection captured well under half of the available headroom -- the ensemble recovered much of it without needing better ranking. Implication for a 19-family project: unweighted ensembling over several plausible source models is robust to bad ranking, which is the failure mode most likely at small n.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: PGDL-MTL9 1.88 C vs PGDL-MTL 2.16 C vs oracle-best-source 1.54 C vs PB0 2.52 C
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 305 target lakes, 145 candidate sources

tier3_unverified.claim: Borrowing a model from other sites beat training on the target's OWN observations only under severe label sparsity, and the crossover point is quantified: a PGDL trained solely on the target lake's data met or exceeded single-source PGDL-MTL at between 5 and 15 target sampling dates, and met or exceeded the PGDL-MTL9 ensemble at between 35 and 40 target sampling dates (12 sparsity levels from 1 to 50 dates, 5 random draws each, over 305 lakes; 221 lakes had >=50 dates, 270 had >=40, all 305 had >=30). Scale-out to 1,882 additional, less-monitored lakes preserved the advantage over the process model: median RMSE 1.80 C (PGDL-MTL9), 2.06 C (PGDL-MTL), 2.29 C (PB0), improving over PB0 for 1,484/1,882 and 1,206/1,882 lakes respectively. Caveat for the Iowa deployment target: at a truly ungauged map pin the crossover is irrelevant (zero local observations, so transfer is the only option), but it means any evaluation site with even ~40 nitrate observations of its own is NOT a fair demonstration of transfer value.
tier3_unverified.effectSize: local-model crossover at 5-15 observations vs single-source transfer, 35-40 observations vs 9-source ensemble; scale-out median RMSE 1.80 vs 2.29 C over 1,882 lakes
tier3_unverified.nBasins: 305 target lakes for the sparsity experiment; 1,882 additional lakes for the scale-out
